items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I am sure that members would wish to
welcome a parliamentary delegation representing the National Assembly of the
Republic of Korea, led by Mr Hong Il Pyo, who are present in the gallery. [ Applause]
Question No. 12 to Minister, 23 July

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: E te Mana Whakawā,
tēnā koe. I seek leave of the House to make a personal explanation to correct an answer
I gave to oral question No. 12 on Thursday, 23 July.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
There is none.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: On Thursday, 23 July in response to a supplementary
question from Darroch Ball regarding an intervie w I undertook with Television New
Zealand’s Q+A programme, I said: “I did never ever answer any question in regard to
Serco, and I have had no conversations with them about any social services.” I have
now had a chance to review the transcript from my inte rview. In that interview I was
asked two questions that cited Serco as an example of a private company that delivers
social services, and I did answer those questions. My apologies. I repeat, however, I
have had no conversations with Serco about the delive ry of social services in New
Zealand. I was making the point in the interview that I would be open to the private
sector delivering some social services if it can be shown it delivers better results.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I
ask you to reflect on that statement just then and to look back at Hansard for last
Thursday. This is precisely why we rais ed the point of order at the time and precisely
why Darroch Ball sought your permission, or the House’s permission, to table that
transcript, because it would have made—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will resume his seat. That is not a point of
order; that will lead to disorder. I will not see the tabling of transcripts in this House. If
members want to seek further information, they have the ability to do so. The point of
tabling is not to make a political point; it is to furth er inform members—[Interruption]
Order! I am speaking to the honourable member Ron Mark. The point of tabling is to
provide further information. If that information is freely available, then I will not be
putting the leave.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I
have a separate point of order to that, and that is regarding the personal explanation
process where the Minis ter is giving a correction. My understanding is that the process
has always been very clear: that Ministers correct what was in error and then leave their
corrections at that. They do not then go on to elaborate the point that they were trying to
make, which is an abuse of that process.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member is correct. Leave is sought to make a personal
explanation. Leave is given by members in the expectation that the explanation given
will be coherent and brief, explaining t he point. I think on this occasion the Minister
5326 Amended Answers to Oral Questions 28 Jul 2015
went on slightly longer than the Minister needed to, but that is for the Minister to call.
The House then reacted accordingly. But, in future, to seek the right to make a personal
explanation is a privilege of the House, and I would expect any member seeking to
make a—[ Interruption] Order! I would expect any member making a personal
explanation to respect that privilege.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is this a fresh point of order, or is it in any way relitigating what has
just been covered? Because if it is, I will treat it very, very seriously by Mr Mark. Think
carefully before you raise—

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Two points—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I just want the first point of order. I am advising the member
before he starts that if it in any way relitigates —[Interruption] Order! I am just warning
the member that if it in any way relitigates —[Interruption] Order! I think the member
had better sit for a minute so I am just absolutely clear. When I reviewed transcripts of
last week there were numerous times when a particular member continued to relitigate
points of order. That, in itself, leads to disorder in this House. So I am giving not only
Mr Mark but all members a warning that if they attempt to relitigate by raising perpetual
points of order, I will treat it very, very seriously and be asking members to leave. Does
the member have a fresh point of order?

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My
point of order is this. Under the Standing Orders that Minister had plenty of time to
come and give this statement prior to the lifting of the House  on the Thursday. I would
ask you to reflect —is it appropriate that we then wait all the way through to the
Tuesday, when the Minister herself could have corrected that error, in accordance with
the Standing Orders—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have heard enough. It is for a member to decide; when they
discover the information they must do so at the earliest convenience. I am not privy to
deciding or knowing when the Minister decided that answer was not correct. It possibly
could have been done Thursday afternoon—that is true —but that is not for me to
determine. The member came into the House at 2 o’clock today, sought leave to make a
personal explanation, and permission was given by the House.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Point of order—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again—[Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I do not need a warning.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will resume his seat —the member will resume his
seat. Again, I want to be fair  to the member, because if he is asked to leave, I do not
want him complaining that he has been asked to leave the Chamber. If it is a fresh point
of order, I am only too happy to hear it, but if it in any way attempts to relitigate where
we have got to si nce the House started at 2 o’clock, I will deal with it severely. A fresh
point of order—the Rt Hon Winston Peters.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. It would be rather obvious —and this point of order is to do with the sequence
of events —that there was a contest as to the veracity  of the matter. A member was
denied a chance to table the document. That would have put the Minister’s staff and the
Minister on alert. But by 10 o’clock—by the close of business that night she had not
done so. That is what the point of order is about. It is the way that a ministerial
statement or an explanation like that should be done and the time frame in which it
should be done. She was on alert to do that. She did not do it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is exactly relitigating w hat I have just said. I now ask
the member to leave the Chamber. I ask the member to leave the Chamber.
Rt Hon Winston Peters withdrew from the Chamber.
28 Jul 2015 Oral Questions 5327
Housing Market—Foreign Ownership of New Zealand Properties
1. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement that “I don’t want to ban foreigners from buying residential
property”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I stand by my full statement, which
was: “We do not support a ban on foreign buyers. We think that’s neither justified nor
likely to be te rribly effective. For the most part, countries don’t have bans but where
they have had them we don’t think they’ve worked very well.”

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Will he sign the Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement, a deal that this
House and the public  have not been allowed to see, if it makes it impossible to stop
people from the US, China, Japan, and elsewhere buying our houses?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the member is a little behind the eight ball because the
reason that a ban may not be applied to a Chinese buyer of a residential property in New
Zealand is as a result of Labour writing the most favoured nation provisions in the
China free-trade agreement and the ratification of the Korean free- trade agreement. It is
a shame that Labour did not think of all this 8 years ago.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Will he sign the Trans -Pacific Partnership agreement if it prevents
his Government or future Governments imposing taxes that apply only to offshore
housing speculators?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member will appreciate that the Trans -Pacific Partnership
agreement is currently under negotiation, so those issues have not been resolved. But I
am confident that future Governments of New Zealand will have plenty of tools in the
tool box when it comes to applying taxes if they so wish to do so.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: How many homes have been sold into overseas ownership since he
said he was concerned about Kiwis becoming tenants in their own land, in 2010; or does
he not know?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not know.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What reports has the Prime Minister received confirming that
banning foreigners from buying residential property does not work?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Last week I received a report from Australia, and I quote:
“The double-whammy of the lowest interest rates since the 1960s and an investor frenzy
has seen Sydney’s median house price smash through the magic AU$1 million mark for
the first time.” The repo rt goes on to note that Sydney’s median house price is now
higher than London’s, and fast approaching New York’s. Investors now have a record
62 percent share of Sydney’s housing market loans. This is the market that, theoretically
at least, bans foreign buyers—something that clearly does not work.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why is he refusing to listen to the overwhelming public demand for
a ban on overseas investors buying our houses and forcing prices out of reach for first -
home buyers here?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We have a far more scientific way of doing things on this side
of the House than looking at whether a name is Chinese and deciding they are the bad
guys. As I said, the reason why we would not be able to ban a Chinese person buyi ng
a—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the Prime Minister. I cannot hear the
answer with that level of interjection.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The reason why they are making that much noise is they know
what I am going to say. The reason why you cannot try to ban a Chinese person is that
Labour wrote it into the law. [Interruption] Yes, you did. Oh yes, you did.
5328 Oral Questions 28 Jul 2015

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Has the Prime Minister seen reports in support of the Government’s
approach to international investment and trade?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. Yes, I have seen two reports. The first one said, and I
quote: “I am a rabid free-trader. I believe in free trade. I am part of a party that has been
pro - free trade and has  initiated many free -trade agreements, including China.” The
second report offered the opposite view. It said: “You may have heard my colleague
describe himself as a passionate free- trader. Well, I could not describe myself in that
way.” The first report w as from Clayton Cosgrove; the second report, a few minutes
later, was from Clare Curran —underlying the deep divisions within the Labour Party.
And that was the tone of their—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Prime Minister will resume his s eat. [ Interruption]
Order! Both sides need to tone down their level of interjection.
Question No. 2 to Minister
Question not asked.
Economic Outlook—Reports
3. DAVID BENNETT (National —Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance:
What reports has he received on the state of the New Zealand economy and what do
these reports show?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: On Fr iday Statistics New Zealand
published merchandise trade data. Merchandise exports in the year to June totalled
$48.5 billion—up $2.8 billion, or 6 percent, on the same period 2 years earlier. The
figures indicate that overall exports to China increased 2.9 percent in June compared
with the same month a year earlier. That happened because gains in the export of non-
dairy produce such as meat and fruit outweighed the impact of a decline in the value of
whole-milk powder exports to the world’s second-largest economy.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What other reports has he received that indicate that the economy is
expanding at a solid, sustainable rate?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Part of the report from Statistics New Zealand was that the
annual value of fruit exports reached an all -time high of $2 billion in the year ended 30
June. That is one of many non- dairy sectors benefiting from the reduction in the
exchange rate and flat to falling interest rates, which are underpinning continued
moderate growth in the New Zealand economy. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I just need to ask for a bit more
cooperation from the left -hand side, otherwise I am going to have to ask somebody to
leave.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What factors support a positive outlook for the New Zealand
economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: A number of factors are supporting the growing economy:
strong inwards migration, including, for the first time, net inflows from Australia to
New Zealand; a stable fiscal outlook; continued growth of the construction and services
sectors; and New Zealand’s high labour force participation. Of course, all these factors
are subject to the usual risks that an open, globalised economy faces, but just becaus e
some of those risks eventuate some of the time, it does not mean that the economy is not
continuing to grow. We are on track for moderate sustainable growth of 2 to 3 percent.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Has the Minister received data about international visitor arrivals?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, because tourism is currently either our largest or
second-largest export, depending on which month you measure it in. Data published last
week showed that international visitor arrivals numbered 177,000 last month, and that is
9 percent higher than in June 2014. This, of course, is very positive for people with jobs
28 Jul 2015 Oral Questions 5329
in industries that are servicing our international guests. The downward correction in the
Kiwi dollar will underpin the c ompetitiveness of our tourism industry, which, I repeat,
is either our largest or our second -largest export industry and looks to be doing fairly
well.
Health, Minister—New Zealand Health Strategy
4. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Minister of Health :
When was he or his office first briefed on the contents of the draft New Zealand Health
Strategy?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker.
Last November I asked officials to commence work on refreshing the New Zealand
Health Strategy, which had not been updated since the year 2000. Since that time I have
met regularly with officials to discuss the direction of the strategy. Following extensive
engagement and input from a wide range of stakeholders, I received the first written
draft of the strategy on 3 July.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of that answer, when he decided to update the New
Zealand Health Strategy did he have any discussions with the Director -General of
Health on what needed to be reviewed, including funding and governance arrangements
for district health boards?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I talk to the director-general about a wide range
of subjects, and of course funding, going into your first Budget as health Minister, is
going to form a core part of those discussions. What else would one expect?

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How could he be unaware of proposed changes to district health
boards’ structures and funding when his Director -General of Health—not a third party,
as he claimed —had, firstly, been briefing him on progress since the beginning of the
month, and, secondly, district health board chairs and chief executive officers had been
given the recommendations in the leaked reports 2 weeks ago?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The member is confusing three different
reviews there. Basically, the funding review and the stolen capacity and capability
review are reviews commissioned by the Director -General of Health. So t hey are his
reviews; he receives the recommendations. He was about to brief me, and then, of
course, the report was stolen by Mrs King’s contact.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I take exception to the last
remark that the member made. I have no contact who stole any documents.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The way forward, to settle the House, is that I am going to
ask the Minister to withdraw that remark, but personally I did not think it was in a ny
way a reflection on the member herself. But can I ask the Minister simply to withdraw
that part about a stolen paper.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Well, Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No—

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I withdraw.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: If he is now ruling out any changes to district health board
governance arrangements, why did he allow papers to go out with proposed changes he
did not agree with, say he had not read the report, and then blame the Director -General
of Health, calling him a third party? I mean, is that incompetence or laziness?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: No, that is completely incorrect. The directo r-
general was not called a third party. If you want to know what incompetence and
laziness is, it is a Minister who doubles the budget and does 2,000 fewer operations,
5330 Oral Questions 28 Jul 2015
who culls 30,000 patients from waiting lists, and who sends 760 people to Australia for
cancer treatment—and that Minister was Annette King. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: No, that is not going to save him either. Is he now taking a
whole-of-Government approach to sensitive issues by getting the communications
manager from the national cyber intelligence office of the Government Communications
Security Bureau to issue rebuttal lines to the media for his Director -General of Health,
or is neither the Minister nor the chief executive officer capable of fronting difficult
issues?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Obviously that is a ridiculous statement. What I
am focusing on is repairing the damage done by Annette King’s $150 million district
health board deficit, which she left behind and which we have now  got down to about
$50 million.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table an email from Cherie Blithe from the
Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, at the national cyber intelligence office,
who sent the email to Radio New Zealand—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It has been described. I just need the date of it.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Yesterday.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that particular email, dated yesterday. Is
there any objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Trans-Pacific Partnership—Potential Outcomes
5. JAMES SHAW (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand by
his statement that “New Zealand is never going to sign up to the TPP unless we believe
it is in New Zealand’s best interests”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Is it in the best interests of New Zealand’s $32 billion information and
communications technology sector that the Trans -Pacific Partnership agreement
requires changes to the Copyright Act that would disallow reverse engineering of
software for interoperability purposes?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Given that the deal has not even been concluded yet, I cannot
go into the individual parts. What I can say is that the overall statement from the
Government stands true. We are not goin g to sign the Trans -Pacific Partnership
agreement unless we believe that it is in the best interests of New Zealand on the
balance of benefits. But I would have thought that the opportunity to have free trade
with the United States, Japan, Mexico, Canada, and other countries puts us in a very,
very strong position.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was in relation to
New Zealand’s $32 billion information and communications technology sector.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I heard the question, and the essence of the answer that I heard from
the Prime Minister is that he cannot really comment on that because the matter is still
under negotiation. That addresses the question.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: Does he agree with the law yer for Vattenfall, the German nuclear
power company currently suing the German Government, that if countries do not want
to be sued by multinational corporations, they should not sign up for agreements
containing investor -State dispute settlement mechanis ms, like the Trans -Pacific
Partnership agreement?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, New Zealand has had investor -State dispute resolution in
successive free -trade agreements, including in the New Zealand -  China Free Trade
28 Jul 2015 Oral Questions 5331
Agreement, signed by the pre vious Labour Government. The important part is having
safeguards included in that.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: If, as calculated by the Parliamentary Library, the benefit to New
Zealand’s dairy sector is only $37 million a year by 2025, or 0.01 percent of GDP,
while the cost to Pharmac from patent extensions is up to $50 million a year, will he
still sign the Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: This is the problem with the Greens’ economic analysis and
research. You are u sing the Parliamentary Library to model something that even I do
not know the details of yet. So guess what? If you put rubbish information in, you get
rubbish information out. Actually, the member, who has done a little bit of this stuff in
his previous career, is way better than this. He would never have done this for a client.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Does he stand by today’s statement about the Trans -Pacific
Partnership and prescription drugs that “patents will run for a little bit longer and that
means the Government will have to pay for the original drug as opposed to the generic”;
if so, can he guarantee that this will not mean higher costs to taxpayers for subsidised
medicines, higher costs to patients for non -subsidised medicines, or a risk that some
medicines will no longer be subsidised due to the increased Budget pressure?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I can guarantee that consumers will not pay more. I think that
it is highly unlikely, actually, that the Government will have to pay any  more through
Pharmac. But on the basis that it had to pay a tiny bit more, the Government would fund
that increase, because, actually, what would end up happening is that the Government
would earn a lot more revenue through tax revenue. That is why David Shearer, Phil
Goff, and David Parker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! That is not necessary for the answer.

items.speaker: James Shaw
items.text: What specifically would it take for him to walk away from the Trans -
Pacific Partnership agreement?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: If I did not believe that the deal was in New Zealand’s best
interests.
State and Social Housing—Tenants Declining Properties
6. BARBARA KURIGER (National—Taranaki - King Country) to the Minister
for Social Housing : What work is being done to ensure social housing is available for
those most in need?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The Government’s social
housing reforms are all about ensuring that there are more social housing places to meet
the needs of vulnerable families. We have introduced reviewable tenancies so that those
who can afford to move on from social housing can do so and make room for someone
who is more in need. So far, 185 people have moved, including 11 who have bought
their own homes. We also have housing support products that help people who are
wanting to go on to the waiting list with bond and moving costs, so that they can go into
private letting, and also for those who are moving out of social housing. We are now
looking at work to address the reasons why people on the register turn down social
houses.

items.speaker: Barbara Kuriger
items.text: How many people have declined an offer of a social house?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: In the year to October 2014, 4,155 offers of a social
house were declined by people on the register, and 3,081 people declined properties .
Some declined multiple properties —for example, 31 people declined a house four
times, and two people declined seven houses each. Twelve percent of those declines, or
498 people, were made without good reason.

items.speaker: Barbara Kuriger
items.text: What kinds  of reasons does she consider are good enough to
decline the offer of a social house?
5332 Oral Questions 28 Jul 2015

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I do not think that people should be declining houses
because they do not like the colour of the door, or because they do not like birds
chirping in the trees next door, or because there are children playing on the street
outside the house and they might ask for money. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is the very last warning that I am giving to the
particular member on my left.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: But these are all reasons that have been given. I
absolutely accept that there are valid reasons for turning down a house, such as wanting
to keep your child at the same school or not wanting to live near  a gang or a P house.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Will the Minister finish her answer.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Every time someone turns down a house that they are
offered, without a good reason, it creates significant delay and means that it takes longer
to get a family who really are in desperate need into that house.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Complete your answer and sit down.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: That situation is not fair, and I am looking to do
something about it.
Economy—Employment
7. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does he stand by his reported statement that the slow -down in growth this
year had come at the right time in the electoral cycle?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes. I do not know whether I actually
used the word “slow -down”. I think I said that it was because the economy is a bit
softer. But that was alongside statements to the effect that we do not want to be a
political party that, as soon as it sees any marke t or global turbulence, starts talking
about spending more, borrowing more, regulating everything, and keeping foreigners
out, which is what the Labour Party has done in the last month.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answer, is he concerned that there are still 146,000
people out of work, 11,000 more than at the time of last year’s election, or is that OK
for those New Zealanders to be doing it tough because it is at the right time in the
electoral cycle?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am not sure what the member is referring to. The number
of people on benefits continues to drop. Today there are 42,000 fewer New Zealand
children in a benefit household than there were 3 years ago. The Government’s social
investment approach to wel fare is increasingly recognised in other developed countries
as very progressive, if not revolutionary.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is he concerned that at least $13 billion will be absent from
regional New Zealand over 2 years as a result of plumme ting dairy prices, or are the job
losses and hard times that go with that just fine in his book, as long as it happens at the
right time in the electoral cycle?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am concerned about that, and having for a number of years
represented an area that has become an intensive dairying area, I know quite a bit about

with New Zealand Bill of Rights Act
Trans-Pacific Partnership—Negotiations

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from the Hon David Parker seeking to
debate under Standing Order 389 a recent declaration by the High Court that the
Electoral (Disqualification of Sentenced Pris oners) Amendment Act 2010 is
inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990. For there to be an urgent
debate, there must be an administrative or ministerial responsibility or the case must be
of recent occurrence. The member, in his application, cites the judgment of the High
Court issued on 24 July as the particular case of recent occurrence. An urgent debate is
a way of holding the Government accountable for an action for which it is responsible.
There must be distinct governmental responsibil ity for the particular case that it is
sought to debate. A decision of the High Court is not a matter for which any Minister
has responsibility. The application is therefore declined.
I have also received a letter from the Rt Hon Winston Peters seeking to debate under
Standing Order 389 the negotiation of the Trans -Pacific Partnership. For an urgent
debate to be granted, there must be a particular case of recent occurrence. Negotiations
on the Trans -Pacific Partnership have been continuing since at least 2010. An ongoing
event is not a particular case of recent occurrence. The application is therefore declined.
5338 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I move, That the New Zealand
Flag Referendums Bill be now read a second time.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: That’s all they’ve got.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is it. That is it.
Tēnā koutou katoa ngā mema o tēnei Whare, arā, te Pāremata o Aotearoa. Tēnā tātou
i tēnei Wiki o Te Reo Māori, ko tāku īnoi kia kaha tātou ki te kōrero Māori.
[Acknowledgments to you all, members of this House —in other words, the New
Zealand Parliament. Greetings to us all in this Māori Language Week. My plea is that
we be robust and speak in Māori.]
This bill ensures that the debate about the New Zealand flag is resolved through a
formal, careful, and respectful process where New Zealanders can have their say. I want
to thank the Justice and Electoral Committee for its thorough consideration of the bill,
and I want to thank those members of the public who made submissions. The committee
received 259 submissions and one form submission representing almost 16,000
individuals.
I would like to address the report of the select committee. The committee has not
recommended major changes to the bill. The majority of the committee recommended
agreement with the structure, procedures, and requirements for the referend ums, which
are fundamentally sound and appropriate for the process. A number of submissions
queried the structure of the referendums and the order of the questions. Many of these
submissions supported the inclusion of a yes/no question about changing the f lag in the
first referendum. The committee considered this, but recommended no change. That is
because a majority of the committee saw the importance of voters being able to give full
consideration to alternative flag designs before deciding whether to kee p or change our
flag. It is pretty logical. People can make an informed decision about whether to change
the flag if they can see what the alternative is.
I would like to briefly touch on two amendments the committee has recommended.
The committee’s first recommendation is to exempt the second flag referendum from
the requirement for a preliminary referendum roll. The purpose of a preliminary roll is
to make an updated electoral roll available for public inspection. However, this will be
done before the fir st referendum, so it is not necessary to require it again before the
second one.
The committee’s second recommendation is to provide a regulated period for
referendum advertising. Members of the House will be familiar with the importance of
the regulated p eriod, and, in parliamentary elections, the significant penalties for
breaching its rules. The regulated period will ensure there is no parliamentary funding
of referendum advertisements advocating that people vote one way or another during
the regulated period. These are fairly technical amendments.
I would like to take the opportunity to briefly mention the activities of the
independent Flag Consideration Panel. The panel’s process was set up and has been
separate from the bill. The panel plays a pretty i mportant role in engaging New
Zealanders on this issue, and will oversee the process of choosing four alternative flag
designs that will be put to voters in the first referendum. Online engagement with the
public has been very high: more than 850,000 visit s to the flag website —somewhat
more, I suspect, than to the Labour Party website during the same time. The panel has
had a number of public workshops, and distributed public information. These
opportunities have been important for people who do not find the internet a comfortable
environment.
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5339
Public suggestions for alternative flag designs closed on 16 July. The flag panel has
received 10,290 flag designs, which indicates some level of public interest. It is now
considering those designs. The panel will report to me in late August with its four
designs, Cabinet will then authorise the four designs to be added to the first referendum
voting paper by Order in Council, and that referendum will be held in November and
December. The preferred alternative design chosen will then be put against the current
flag in the second binding referendum. The Electoral Commission will conduct these
referendums and has robust systems in place, as one would expect.
I am grateful for the input of members of political parties and members of the public
who have participated in the development of this bill. There has been— and certainly in
this House —some robust opinion about whether to change the flag and what kind of
flag to change it to, but I can tell you two of the main reasons I  have heard that are the
wrong reasons. One is that the Opposition members do not like John Key. That is the
main reason they oppose the referendums.
The second reason is that they want to change the flag but they wish they had had the
courage themselves to put forward the proposition. We know that because putting up a
referendum to change the flag is Labour Party policy. The Labour Party has always
prided itself on being the owners of New Zealand —its brand, its identity, its spirit, and
its principles. That may have been the case when Michael Joseph Savage was the Prime
Minister, but in this intellectually bankrupt, unaspirational, modern Labour Party, it
does not own any aspect of our national identity. The National Party, of course, believes
that the people own it. We are not a Government that regards its job as promoting
national identity. What would Governments know that they could add? The people own
it and that is why the people should have a say about whether they want a new flag.
There is a third reason that is a bad reason for opposing this bill, and it is the one that
New Zealand First members have picked—that is, they are simply against New Zealand
being an open, forward- looking, progressive country. They think that New Zealanders
are incapable of making a dangerous decision like whether to change a flag or not. In
fact, so does the Labour Party now. I mean, what is the Labour Party going to say if
New Zealand votes to change the flag? It will condemn it to even more irrelevance than
the track that it is on.
So I look forward to hearing in this debate a debate about the flag and about the
process of picking it. I do not look forward to hearing the whingeing, backward- looking
complaints of the Opposition parties, which lack confidence in New Zealand a nd
aspiration for New Zealanders.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker.
Just when 4.4 million Kiwis have been asked what they stand for, I thought that at least
the Deputy Prime Minister might stand up and tell us what he stood for. He stood there
for half his speech with his hands in his pockets, and he did not tell us a thing. He stood
there—dare I say —whingeing and moaning and carrying on, because the truth is that
New Zealanders do not want this change right now.
There are thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of New Zealanders
who want a banner that reflects and represents the mightiness that is New Zealand, but
they know a bad thing when they see it and they know bad times when they see them.
Many of the delegates who turned up to the National Party conference this weekend, the
weekend just gone —they know a bad thing when they see it, too, which was when the
Minister of Finance stood up to speak to that conference. They knew it was all bad, too.
They were not convinced by a Minister of Finance who stands up and says: “Don’t
worry. The electoral cycle will take care of it all. We’re just OK for 2017.” The same
applies to the flag. This is not a question of the electoral cycle. This is a question about
5340 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
our national identity, but it is a question about the time when New Zealanders are
comfortable with change.
Right now this economy, because of this Government’s appalling economic
mismanagement, is facing some of the most serious headwinds we have seen in a
generation. There is massive loss in the dairy price, massive loss of economic
confidence. You walk up the main street of Whanganui and a quarter of the shopfronts
are now empty. People in Whanganui are concerned, like in many other regions around
New Zealand. People are concerned about the immediate future of New Zealand, and
they want the Government to be there to help. They want the Government to be there to
help with housing, to help with social housing, to provide insulation for housing, to look
after our kids, and to make sure all those kids who are still going hungry in our schools
might get a decent feed, whether for breakfast or lunch. What they do not want at these
difficult times is a Government that has already spent $8 million on a referendum
process without a referendum being held yet, with another $17 million left to go, when
there are greater priorities at stake.
This Government has just got it wrong. If there is any further evidence required, just
about the level of enthusiasm that there is amongst the public in New Zealand about
this, then just look at these figures. They ha d 25 public meetings. These were the
opportunities for mass public engagement. Hundreds of people were expected to turn
up—that is at each meeting, I mean, not across all of them. Across all those meetings,
739 people turned up—an average of 29 per meeting . Do you know how many people
turned up in New Plymouth?

items.speaker: Hon Maggie Barry
items.text: How many on the website?

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Maggie Barry has been to New Plymouth recently, because I
enjoyed sitting alongside her when we opened the iconic Len Lye Centre. But I wonder,
when she looked out at the vast throng of people who turned up at that most iconic
building, whether she realised how many had turned up to the flag referendum meeting.
Eight. Eight people in New Plymouth. The people of New Plymouth are good people.
The people of New Plymouth are good people —they know iconic identity when they
see it because they have now got it on their front doorstep—but they do not want a flag
change. That is why eight people turning up to a meeting designed for several hundred
tells you that people do not want a flag change. They do not want this referendum, and
as you go up and down the country—15 people in some other place, 22 somewhere else;
an average of 29 at each meeting.
What about the website submissions? The Deputy Prime Minister says: “Well we’ve
had thousands of submissions. Over 10,000 submitted new designs of the flag.” We
know what they look like, because Parliament was treated to the spectacle of some of
those flags last week: a sheep w ith a rainbow coming out of its bottom —and that pretty
much sums up the National Party. That is the state it is in —a pack of sheep. It wants
something flash and fancy. It will not deal with the methane issue in our agriculture
sector so it is left up to th e flag designers amongst us to try to get a message to the

items.speaker: National Party
items.text: will you please do something about the real issues? That is what that
flag design represents. Then there were others: meat pies, Jelly Tips, jandals, kiwi, all
the rest of it. There is nothing wrong with those. Unfortunately, the Leader of the House
has gone, because I know that he will have a fascination with some of those designs.
But this is where people are at —they do not take it seriously. They do not take it
seriously, because they have got other priorities. The rest of New Zealand,
overwhelmingly, has other priorities at this difficult time in our history. This is not the
time—when people are disengaged, when people are concerned, and when people are
anxious about unemployment, about the state of our economy, about what is happening
to our farming sector, and about what is happening in the regions. They do not need a
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5341
$17 million referendum that asks the wrong questions in the wrong order. If we are
going to have a referendum we should have at least turned it round and asked in the
right order. But people have spoken loudly and clearly: they do not want the change
right now.
That is not a poor reflection on New Zealanders, many of whom would like
something different, many of whom would like a change. Many of them want a change
to the national anthem, too, because they are sick of singing a dirge every time you turn
up to a festive occasion. Most of them sing along to the Australian national anthem
before they sing along to our own.  They want something different, but they do not want
it at a time —and they do not want this Government, which parades itself as the great
financial managers and the great financial responsibility people of the generation,
spending $17 million—when this country can ill afford it.
We have never been under greater pressure financially. This economy has never been
under greater pressure, and yet the Minister of Finance, the Deputy Prime Minister, has
the temerity to stand up in this House and sell us a dodgy bi ll of goods—a dodgy bill of
goods: a flag that they do not know and an identity they cannot be clear about. This is
the issue that New Zealanders are clear about: if this Government cared about New
Zealanders, if this Government actually started treating N ew Zealanders as if they
mattered, it would see the writing on the wall. It would see the sheep bottoms and the
rainbows, and it would say: “Now is not the time.” It would be honest with New
Zealanders and say it is time for a strategic withdrawal, we can come back to this
another time, we will respect the wishes of New Zealand and we will abandon the
referendum and save the $17 million, and we will use it for something useful.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I want to thank the select committee
members from all sides of the House for their consideration in this New Zealand Flag
Referendums Bill. We had a good process with good engagement by the public and
enjoyed many submissions. In fact, we enjoyed many suggestions for alternative flags. I
think that comes to the heart of why this process is so important for New Zealanders,
because it gives them—it gives New Zealanders —the opportunity to think about and to
come to a view on what they think best represents us as a country in terms of a flag.
We had a number of submitters, some of whom were entertaining and some of whom
gave us some very impassioned views on how they saw New Zealand. I think that is the
essence of this subject. It is that through the select committee process, and also through
the flag consideration process, which is happening at the same time, it gave New
Zealanders an opportunity to record what they believed an alternative flag might look
like.
That brings me back to the structur e of the New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill. It
was our job in the select committee to consider the structure around the discussion—the
structure around the two referendums. If I refer to the bill, schedules 1 and 2 outline
what the referendum questions are  going to be. In the first question, which is the first
voting paper for the first flag referendum, it asks: “If the New Zealand flag changes,
which flag would you prefer?” —if the New Zealand flag changes, which flag would
you prefer? That question is asking people to first consider this in their minds: “OK, if it
changes”. It immediately asks a meaningful question of the public, which is: if it
changes. The answer might be: “All right, so if it changes; you’re right, that is
something I have to think about.” Then the second part of that first question is: which of
these four alternatives do you prefer? So people are then directed to make an informed
choice. That is the first question.
The second referendum then asks the question—it puts up the existing New  Zealand
flag, which we have had since 1908, and the preferred alternative, and then asks them:
5342 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
“Of these two alternatives, which do you prefer?”. It is an informed choice, and it is the
choice that is put out to the New Zealand public to make.
It is inter esting, is it not, that the online process for gathering alternative flags has
been a pretty busy process. There have been more than 10,000 alternative flag designs
published, which is really interesting —10,000 different flag designs. I know that all of
us who are interested in these things have had a look at those alternative flags from time
to time, and we are coming to a view, and it will be an informed view because of the
structure of this bill. There have been 2.7 million views of the flag gallery and more
than 850,000 online visits, and so this has been a particularly successful online
investigation, which, of course, is very appropriate, given that this is such a visual
question. What do we want for New Zealand? Do we want New Zealand to reflect our
rich history? Do we want New Zealand to reflect our modern, forward- looking, open,
progressive nature? Well, the structure of this bill gives New Zealanders the opportunity
to do just that.
During the consideration of the select committee we did recommend some changes,
one of which was the requirement for a preliminary referendum roll for the second
referendum. The preliminary referendum roll for the first referendum makes a public
roll of electors available for people to check, first of all, that they are on the roll and,
secondly, that their details are correct. It was the view of the majority of the select
committee that because the second referendum was to happen in fairly short order, it
would be an unnecessary expense and an unnecessary process to make  the preliminary
referendum roll for the second referendum available.
The select committee, by majority, also recommended to Parliament that a regulated
period be inserted into the bill to prohibit members of Parliament from spending
parliamentary funding on referendum advertising. This is consistent with the Electoral
Act and provides for a level playing field in the consideration of what will be a very
focused discussion, no doubt, leading up to the referendums. So the committee agreed
to insert that and make that recommendation.
We did consider other aspects that were brought to us. Some submitters said to the
committee that they believed that the word “Aotearoa” should be included in the bill.
We considered whether the title of the bill should contain “Aotearoa”—of course, it is
Māori Language Week. But it was determined, due, really, to an issue of a technical
nature, which is that the New Zealand flag is known as “the New Zealand Flag” within
the Flags, Emblems, and Names—
Denis O’Rourke: Really?

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I know it is difficult for New Zealand First. I know it is difficult,
because this is a little bit technical, but just breathe through your noses, boys, and you
might get it. So in terms of the Flags, Emblems, and Na mes Protection Act 1981 it
would therefore have been a little inconsistent.
The timing of the flag consideration process was also raised by some submitters, and
the committee considered the views, which were strongly given to us, particularly by
the RSA an d other members who had the view that the consideration in this year was
inappropriately close to the Gallipoli campaign centenary and Anzac Day
commemorations. The reality of it is that it does not matter when these referendums
were timed; they were always going to be adjacent to some national celebration or some
national event. It was felt, and I agree entirely, that it is far more appropriate to be
having this consideration away from an election year, because it would either be
eclipsed by or maybe eclip se the consideration in a general election. We believe, by
majority, that it is much more appropriate to give these referendums their own space.
The committee considered at the same time a petition from the Hon Trevor Mallard,
who, no doubt, will make a c ontribution on that petition in the House today and in
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5343
subsequent debates. The committee listened again carefully and with respect to Mr
Mallard’s petition and the petitioners calling for the New Zealand Government to
include in the first referendum a question asking New Zealanders whether they wanted a
change of flag or not. It was considered but, by majority, the committee held the view
that the order of questions as introduced provided for a more informed choice and a
more informed consideration of the question at hand.
I am very pleased to speak in the second reading of the New Zealand Flag
Referendums Bill. I believe that the structure that is being proposed in this bill is the
right structure to provide New Zealanders with an informed choice. It is an  opportunity
to provide New Zealanders with the opportunity to consider where we stand in the
world, what New Zealand stands for, and what the alternatives are that might reflect
who and what we stand for now. Do they reflect us as the New Zealand we want to be?
Do they reflect us as an outward- looking, progressive, open country? I think this bill
puts the structure in place, and now it is up to the people. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MAL LARD
items.text: Ngā mihi o te rā. I never
thought that I would see another select committee process as bad as the one that was run
by Todd McClay when he chaired the Finance and Expenditure Committee, but under
Jacqui Dean, the process for this bill has been an absolute disgrace. I want to name the
members Jacqui Dean, Jono Naylor, Chris Bishop, Alfred Ngaro, and the Hon Louise
Upston. They were the National Government members on this committee who decided
that 747 people who had asked to be heard by the committee would be denied the right
to be heard. Those members voted to give submitters 5 minutes to speak. They were the
members who gave the very few submitters whom they allowed to come to the
committee 5 minutes to speak. To be fair, there was an exception. The New Zealand
RSA—the Royal New Zealand Returned and Services’ Association —was allowed 10
minutes. The representatives of the returned soldiers —people who had fought under the
flag—were allowed only 10 minutes before the committee to expres s the views of their
tens of thousands of returned members.
This Parliament has enough trouble with its public relations that when submitters to
committees are treated in such a disgraceful manner by members of the National
Government, who acted as if they  knew everything and did not want to listen, this
Parliament’s reputation will be diminished further. I want to say that Jacqui Dean, Chris
Bishop, Jono Naylor, Alfred Ngaro, and Louise Upston were too damn lazy to sit the
select committee during the 3 weeks of adjournment. They were too lazy to sit the select
committee during the 3 weeks of adjournment, in order to hear the people who wanted
to be heard. When that occurs and when 747 people who ask to be heard are not, then
this Parliament’s reputation will be in tatters.
The main point that the RSA representatives wanted to make and that the people
whom they had emailed and who had emailed submissions back wanted to make was
that they thought that the timing was appalling. They thought that having both ref erenda
during the period that we are commemorating the First World War was inappropriate. In
April 1916 the entire Massey Cabinet went to the Pētone railway station for the first
annual official Government commemoration of Anzac Day. The entire Cabinet was
there. And what is going to happen in the couple of weeks before the centenary of that,
and with the flag that was raised along with the Australian flag at the Pētone railway
station? What is going to happen? This Government is promoting that that is when a
decision on the flag should be made. The timing is wrong. The timing is wrong for lots
and lots of reasons.
On the yes/no question, on the that day it was considered by the advisory group, by
the cross-party group, there was only one dissenting voice —and it was one of doubt —
as to whether this should be a yes/no vote. The dissenting voice —and it was a bit of a
5344 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
wobble—belonged to Jonathan Young. He was not sure whether he had checked with
Bill English, he said. Every other party that was present on the day said that there
should be a yes/no vote, as there was with the MMP referendum. Even those toadies
who rely on the National Government to deliver their seats —Mr Seymour and Mr
Dunne—even those two members said: “Of course this should be a yes/no vote. New
Zealanders should have their say early in the process, and if we can save money, then
we should.” But the National Government has decided to bulldoze its approach through
the House and to not trust New Zealanders, as it trusted New Zealanders when we
brought in MMP, to say, as part of the first referendum process, whether they want to
consider a change or not.
I think it is fair to say that Labour went into the first reading of this bill opposing it
but with the hope that the bill could be improved, through the process, to the point that
we could support it going further. There are a number of us, myself included, who think
that we should change our flag eventually—eventually we should.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Proper process.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: We want a proper process, we want the timing to be
right, and we do not want the referenda to be rorted. We do not want it to be biased in
the way that John Key wants for his vanity project. When we are being told that there is
not enough money for food in schools, that there is not enough money for rape crisis
centres, and that there is not enough money to fix up State houses that have gaping
holes in them, we think that this spending on a vanity project for the Prime Minister is
something that is inappropriate. We believe that the referenda are poorly worded.
I just want to ask the members opposite whether they really think that spending on
hall hire, meeting fees, and advertising for meetings —$2,300 for every person who
turned up to those meetings—is good value for money. What sort of efficiency—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: That’s a lot of kids’ lunches.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Well, the member says that that is a lot of kids’
lunches. It is a lot of insulat ion. It would fix the holes in the State flats in Pētone —the
total amount that was set there —that have been waiting for 5 years. Members opposite
are so arrogant, notwithstanding that and notwithstanding the shift. My understanding is
that about 5 years ag o, when Lloyd Morrison was leading a campaign, there was a
majority in New Zealand in favour of changing the flag. A couple of years later, it went
from about 50 percent in favour down to about 30 percent in favour. My understanding
is that we have now got to the point that it has gone below 10 percent. It has gone below
10 percent in favour of changing the flag. So the question I have got is: why are we
continuing with this?
One of the important things for Governments is to work out, at some point, when
they have got it wrong. It is important to work out when they have got it wrong and
when it is the time to beat a strategic retreat, to say that we have listened. We have
listened to the select committee process. We have listened to the former soldiers. We
have listened to the people who said that there is a higher priority for the money, and we
will send this bill on, we will leave it on the Order Paper, and we will leave it there for 5
years. We will leave it there until after the commemoration of the First World War, and
we will bring it—well, the National Government will not, of course—bring it back up at
that stage for further consideration. That, I think, would be an honest approach, it would
be a fair approach, and it would be acknowledging what is happening.
At the end of my speech, I do want to acknowledge that right back at the beginning
of the process the Rt Hon Winston Peters was right and I was wrong. I believed the
National Government —I believed Bill English and I believed John Key —when they
said that they were open and would take into account what the cross -party committee
said. What they did was they did not take this into account, as far as the membership of
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5345
the advisory group was concerned. Most of the advisory group are good people, but it
was balanced out with National Government hacks who were not recommended by the
cross-party committee. The other question is that no one else in the committee, with
only the dithering of Jonathan Young, supported this shape of referendum, but because
it is John Key’s vanity project, they have decided to rort the process. They have decided
to spend the money. As a result of that, all over New Zealand people are saying:
“Generally, I trust John, but on this one, he’s just got it wrong.”

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: I just want to start this contribution by putting the
New Zealand flag into a little bit of context. From some of the speeches that we have
heard from the other side of the House and some of the debate t hat we have heard from
submitters at different times, you would begin to think that this was the only flag that
New Zealand had ever had. How could you ever possibly change the New Zealand flag,
because it is the only one we have ever had! What we do know is that this is in fact the
third flag that New Zealand has had. But I think there is a really important thing to
notice about the three flags that New Zealand has had. None of those flags were voted
on or chosen by the people of New Zealand. Those flags w ere decided on by the
Government of the day, which decided to choose the flag, which decided to tell the
people of New Zealand what their flag would be. It denied them the opportunity of
choosing their flag.
It does not really matter, to a certain degree, whether you want to keep the flag or
whether you want to change the flag. This referendum gives New Zealanders the
opportunity to choose their national emblem, their national symbol. It is not the
Government’s choice. We have got these people who are sayin g “Don’t have a
referendum. Don’t give the people the choice. Don’t let them choose to keep this flag or
perhaps choose another one.”, and they are simply going by the original decision of
1905 to impose this flag on the people of New Zealand. Let us face it. We are not
saying it is a horrible flag. We are not saying that we are not proud of our country. What
we are saying is that this is an important issue of national significance, and it is one that
the people of New Zealand will get to make a choice on.
I think it is really interesting too that we are told that the people of New Zealand do
not want this. This is based on opinion polls. I am just wondering whether the members
opposite think we should just go by opinion polls. In February of last year the C olmar
Brunton poll said that the National Party would have 51 percent of the vote if an
election were held. I am wondering whether the members opposite would have been
happy, at that point, to concede and just say: “OK, let’s give the National Party 51
percent, because that’s what the polls are saying. That’s what the people of New
Zealand want, and so therefore we’ll let the National Party have 51 percent of the vote.”
I do not think they would have been quite so happy to quote the polls at that point. I do
not think they would have been quite so happy to let the choice of New Zealanders be
determined by a poll at that point. But, no, when it suits the agenda of members
opposite, when it suits their desire to impose on the people of New Zealand what their
flag should or should not be, then they want to go by the polls. They do not want to give
the people of New Zealand the right to choose their emblem. They do not want to do
that, because they know better. I can tell you that we do not claim to know better, and
that is the purpose behind this referendum. The purpose behind this referendum is to
allow the people of New Zealand to indicate to us what they would like for their
national emblem. It is what they would like to take forward.
Now that we are bringing this issue through, now that it is on the table and we have
got this bill before us, there has been a lot of talk about the order of the questions. They
have been saying that we should give people a yes/no vote for this one first, before we
ask about the others. I have spoken to quite a few people, and am probably in this
5346 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
position myself as well, who say that they are open to the idea of changing the New
Zealand flag. I am open to the idea of changing the New Zealand flag, but it will all
depend, I know, fr om my way of thinking and the thinking of lots of the other people
whom I have talked to, on what the alternatives are. Lots of people would say “Well, if
you gave me a yes/no question at the moment I might say no.”, because they are
concerned that it migh t end up being a sheep with a rainbow coming out the back of it.
If I had the choice between a sheep with a rainbow coming out of its bottom and the
current New Zealand flag, I think I would vote for the current New Zealand flag. I am
pretty sure we all wo uld—pretty sure we all would. However, if we were going to get
the choice between the New Zealand flag and one of those Kyle Lockwood designs,
then perhaps I might be more likely to choose, or I might be more likely to choose
something that at least has some other symbols of New Zealand on it.
I just want to draw people’s attention to one of our submitters, who I think summed
up the idea of why it is important for us to do things in this process. We got a
submission via teleconference from a young man calle d Jordan Ward. He raised the
following concerns, so if you will just excuse me, I want to read out what he said. He
believes, in respect of the yes/no question, and I think I agree with him, that “electors
voting ‘no’ to change in the first referendum” —or in the first part of that referendum —
“may be less likely to express their preferences for an alternative design”, which might
come after. What we need to do is we need to simplify this. We need to keep it simple.

items.speaker: We need to say to people
items.text: “If New Zealand w ere to change its flag, which one would
you prefer?”. It is a pretty simple question and it is pretty easy to understand. There is
no problem whatsoever. At that point, whichever flag is the winner would be run off
against the current New Zealand flag. It is really simple and really easy to understand. It
is really easy to comprehend. If you put that yes/no question at the very front end of all
of that, it makes life a little trickier because those people who have not yet made up
their mind whether or not t hey do want to change the flag, because they are waiting to
see the alternatives, will then be able to vote accordingly.
I did a little bit of a search on New Zealand logos and symbols. People will have
heard this comment made before. How many people have got a T -shirt with a New
Zealand flag on it in the cupboard? Not too many. How many people have got a cap that
has the New Zealand flag on it? Not too many. But if we look around, we see the
symbolism that is most commonly associated with New Zealand, and we can look at a
few different things. For example, the New Zealand Air Force aircraft have a kiwi on
them. That is what is on the side of our New Zealand Air Force planes. New Zealand
Trade and Enterprise, for example, has a sort of a fern design. Actuall y, what is on our
New Zealand war graves is a silver fern. In fact, even if we look at an organisation such
as the New Zealand Labour Party, within its logo it incorporates a fern, not necessarily
the New Zealand flag. So we need to have something, I belie ve, that is easily
identifiable. That is just a personal belief. I think it is great. I think we need to give the
opportunity for people to decide what is important to them.
There have been a lot of great events that have happened over the years, and we
associate the current New Zealand flag with them. For example, when Edmund Hillary
climbed Mount Everest—oh, wait; he did not take the New Zealand flag with him, did
he? He took the Union Jack with him. So we look at things like that. We see Olympians
draped in our New Zealand flag and we feel proud. We feel proud of them because of
what they have achieved, not necessarily because of the flag that they have got around
them. Whatever we choose, whatever the people of New Zealand decide is going to be
the most appropriate emblem to drape our Olympians in and to mark significant events
with, that is what is going to be important. It is going to be important that it symbolises
what is at the heart of our nation. That is why this debate, to my mind, has been so
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5347
important, because regardless of whether we keep this flag or change this flag, our
nation will have been through, hopefully, a very mature discussion—well, apart from
the banter that I hear from the other side of the House, which is not particularly mature
or helpful.
But we have been hearing some very good debate across our nation about what it
means to be a New Zealander, what it means to be a Kiwi, and what is important to us
as a nation. I hope that whatever flag we choose, whether it is the one that we have
currently got or a new flag, we will be stronger as a nation, more united as a nation, and
we will have a better understanding of who it is that we are, what we represent, and we
will be able to move forward to be a great nation —an even greater nation than we are
now. I look forward to the outcome of this bill, to the outcome of the referenda, and
then for us to be able to move on together. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: E  te  M ā ng a i o  te Whare, tēnā koe. There is an
ugly word that is used by political operatives and political spin doctors. It is also used
quite a lot in the public relations industry and by those who have an interest in
manipulating public opinion. It is a word that is the  very opposite of substance. It is the
word “optics”. Optics is all about how something looks. It is not about what the reality
of something is; it is not about what the real content of something is. Optics is all about
how it looks. What kind of an appear ance would it give? How would something look to
a person if they were passing by it and did not really look at it closely? The bill that we
have in front of us today is all about optics. It is all about how it looks, and it is all about
the legacy of our P rime Minister. What he wants to give is an appearance of substance.
What he wants to give is an appearance of being a progressive, forward -looking,
aspirational Prime Minister leading an aspirational, forward -looking Government. He
wants to use this symbol  and this referendum on the flag in order to get the right
optics—how does it look?
How would it look to a person who was not really paying any attention? It would
look like: “Well, the Prime Minister is forward -looking; he wants to change the flag.”
He wants to adopt a modern, aspirational, forward -looking flag, as we have heard from
all the National Government speakers —a flag that enshrines our national identity. But
by changing the flag, what are we really changing? Are we changing the fact that our
head of State is, in fact, a foreigner; that our head of State is, in fact, chosen by birth;
and that our head of State is, in fact, a hereditary monarch? By choosing a new flag,
does it change any of those fundamental constitutional arrangements? No—the Prime
Minister does not want to deal with that. That is hard; that is leadership.
If you want to have a constitutional republic in New Zealand, if you want to be a
Prime Minister who actually wants to make New Zealand constitutionally independent,
that would ta ke leadership of substance, not leadership of optics. This bill is about
optics. It is about how it would look. How would it look if we adopted a new flag? It
would look like this was a Government that was addressing some fundamental issues
about our const itution because we were changing the flag. It would look like a
Government, perhaps, that was addressing some of the fundamental issues of our
identity, like our relationship with tangata whenua and the Treaty of Waitangi. No, it is
just changing a piece o f cloth and the pattern on a piece of cloth. The constitutional
structure will remain exactly the same. So we will have a hereditary head of State.
Hereditary heads of State are very strange things. I mean, imagine, for example, if
you had an accident this  afternoon and you had to go to hospital and you said: “Well, I
need heart surgery, but it’s all right, because the father” —or mother —“of my heart
surgeon was a heart surgeon. They are a hereditary heart surgeon, so I’m sure that they
are going to do a rea lly good job.” Ha! A hereditary heart surgeon! Honestly, would
anyone here say: “I’m going to go and give my body over to a hereditary heart surgeon,
5348 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
because their father or mother was a very good heart surgeon, so I think they must be a
good heart surgeon as well.”? When I get my hair cut —I am going to get my hair cut in
a week or so; it needs to be every now and then—would I say: “Oh well, my
hairdresser’s mother or father was a very good hairdresser, so I’m sure that they will do
an excellent job.”? But when it comes to the constitution and to the head of State, we
say: “No, no, it’s all right. We are going to hand over the office of head of State to a
person who was chosen by birth.” Ha, ha! By birth—that is right. That is how we are
choosing our head of  State. Not by a democratic process; they did not have to go
through a test to prove how good they are. I was not: “Oh, yeah—if you are good on the
constitution, let’s test you on the constitution.” No, we choose them by birth.
This bill, which gives the appearance of dealing with some really substantive issues
about our nation—the flag —does not deal with any of the really substantive issues that
confront our country. From John Key’s point of view, that is the beauty of this
referendum. It is manipulation of public opinion. It gives the appearance of substance
without actual substance. It looks like the Prime Minister is addressing the big issues of
the day—the big issues of the nation. Well, the Prime Minister is doing nothing of the
sort, and that is exac tly what he needs, because what he really wants is a fourth term as
Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister talks about independence from the United Kingdom —“This flag
will symbolise our independence from the United Kingdom.” Actually, it will do
nothing of the  sort. The head of State will still be a British person —Charles. He is a
perfectly nice fellow. In fact, on green issues, he is pretty good, you would have to say.
I have got a lot of sympathy for Prince Charles on green issues. But as for being a
person who should be the head of State of New Zealand— I do not think that is the right
way to go about it.
Think about the fundamental issues around the Bill of Rights. The courts have just
ruled that this Parliament breached the constitution of New Zealand by say ing that
prisoners are not allowed to vote. Are we going to talk about that?

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Can’t debate that here, though.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: We cannot even have an urgent debate about that. The
Speaker said “No, no—that’s not serious enough.” The fact that according to the courts
this Parliament breached the constitution of New Zealand by taking away prisoners’
right to vote is not important enough to have an urgent debate. It is certainly not
important enough to ha ve a referendum about! For goodness sake, we have got to have
one about the flag—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is now relitigating a finding that has
already been committed to the House by the Speaker. It is not up for debate. The
member should get back to this debate, which is about the flag referendum, please.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Thank you for your wise advice, Mr Deputy Speaker. In
terms of the flag, the Prime Minister has been very clear that he wants to have a debate
about optics—that is what he wants —not about substance, not about the New Zealand
Bill of Rights Act, and no t about the constitution. Even though the Prime Minister talks
about the constitution in relation to this flag, Mr Deputy Speaker will not let me talk
about the constitution in relation to this flag. But the Prime Minister, of course, does. He
gives the appearance that this is about substance; it is nothing of the sort.
The process itself is manipulative. That is the giveaway. When we had the MMP
referendum, the first question was: do you want to have first past the post or MMP?

items.speaker: You had to decide
items.text: do you wa nt to keep first past the post? If the majority said yes, we
kept it. The majority voted for change. When we had the second MMP referendum, the
first question was: do you want to keep MMP or not? It was a yes/no decision. But with
this referendum on the flag, the Prime Minister is purposely manipulating the process to
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5349
push it towards the outcome he wants. That is manipulative. That is about optics. That is
about spin. That is about Government by spin. That is about Government by optics. It is
trying to manipulate the people of New Zealand in order to get the outcome that it
wants.
The honest question is this —first question of the referendum —do you want to
change the flag? My answer to that question is yes. I want to change a lot of things,
actually. I want t o have a proper democracy, which is what a constitutional republic is
all about. I want to make sure that this Parliament operates within the constitution of
New Zealand and the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. I want to do a lot of things. But
on the quest ion of how to do this flag referendum, it is manipulative —in the way that
the Government has set up the referendum question in order to push it towards the result
it wants.
As a matter of fact, when the first referendum comes along and you have got to pick
between four different kinds of flags, if you do not want to change the flag, you are not
likely to participate in that referendum. Is there a quorum? What is the quorum? Ten
people could participate in this referendum. Is there any quorum for this thing, I ask the
National Government members over there? What if 10 people vote in this referendum?
What if the turnout is 20 percent? What if the turnout in that first referendum is 10
percent?

items.speaker: Louisa Wall
items.text: No mandate.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Where will the mandate be for this new flag, then? There
will not be one. So this is all about optics. This referendum is all about optics, and it is
all about making the Prime Minister look like he cares for something.
May I remind you that Keith  Locke put up a bill —the Head of State Referenda
Bill—and the Prime Minister blocked it from even going to a select committee. That
would have meant a true debate about our identity and a true debate about our
constitutional arrangements, but John Key said: “No, we will not have a real debate. I’m
not going to allow that. We can have a debate around my flag proposal” —which is all
about optics and deception—“but we cannot have a real debate.”
One of my reading habits lately has been Tom Paine, and there is a great Tom Paine
quote about the monarchy. Tom Paine said that “a long habit of not thinking a thing
wrong gives it a superficial appearance of being right”. He was talking about the
monarchy, and that was just before the American Revolution. This is exact ly the same
situation we find ourselves in today—a long habit of not thinking a thing wrong gives it
the appearance of being right. We should address the real constitutional issues facing
our country —constitutional monarchy, constitutional republic —rather than getting
caught up in the Prime Minister’s optics around this referendum on a flag.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : The Government should be withdrawing this
unpopular bill. The submissions to the Justice and Electoral Committee showed the
magnitude of the degree of unpopularity of the bill. There were literally hundreds of
submissions against it. However, only a few were actually heard, because of the
