arrogance of the National members on the select  committee. The consultation process
was no better. It showed very little public pressure for any change at all, and the truth is
that this Government is pushing this bill through against public opinion, not following
it. The roadshow that accompanied the public consultation process was an absolute
farce, and you would have got more people turning out to a snake oil auction than went
to that particular farce. There was also only modest response to the internet -based
facility for comment—only very modest response.
Many submitters have also, properly, been concerned about the total cost —$25.7
million—being spent on this farcical process. Those people said that it was a waste of
taxpayers’ money, for no gain. They said to spend the money elsewhere. They said to
5350 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
spend it on new homes, on education, and on better health services. Of course, there will
be many, many other costs if this process to change the flag actually succeeds. It will
include a large number of official publications and emblems —even including dr iver’s
licences, for example—not to mention the millions needed to run the referendums and
for the advertising of them. Passports will have the wrong flag on them, and all of those
will have to change. And there are many, many other costs that are almost i mpossible to
quantify for businesses and other organisations that will need to change the flags on
their promotional material. Those costs have been estimated by some as likely to exceed
$100 million. That is the true cost of this exercise—that is the true cost.
Many submitters were also opposed to the process of holding the two referendums.
Using preferential voting, the first referendum will determine, from only four
alternatives to be prescribed, which alternative flag design is preferred. The second wil l
determine whether the alternative flag or the current flag should be the one that is
accepted. Only if voters decide in the second referendum that the New Zealand flag is to
change will that then lead to further legislation to actually do away with the current flag.
The point is that there could have been one referendum only. If there is going to be a
referendum, one would be enough, simply by adding the current New Zealand flag to
the four that are going to be put up in the first referendum. So this is a  deeply flawed
process, and the Government has got it totally the wrong way round. Before spending
millions of dollars on the two planned referendums and before appointing any panels or
incurring any other expenses, there should have been one referendum only. That
referendum should have asked the simple question: “Do you want a new national flag to
replace the current one?”. Simply that question alone would have been enough, and only
if the answer had been yes, by a majority, would it have been justifiable to spend any
money taking the matter any further.
The process set out in this bill appears to be a way for the Government to rig the
result—nothing less than that. It is rigging the result, getting what it wants —a new
flag—by having only four options decided first. That pre -empts the primary question,
which is simply: “Does anyone want a new flag at all?”. Instead, we have this ludicrous,
back to front process as a blatant means of trying to influence the result. New Zealand
people will see through it and w ill tell this Government, in no uncertain terms, where to
put its new flag proposal.
Many submitters have asked, validly, why we would even consider a new flag. The
current one is not out of date. It is as appropriate today as it was in 1908, when it was
officially adopted. In fact, it is actually a young flag when compared with many others.
It represents, through having the Union Jack, the British heritage of New Zealand. The
English language, legal system, and culture, and the Westminster system of government
are just as much Kiwi as they are British. The flag represents that perfectly, and it also
represents our Pacific and Māori culture. The Southern Cross on a blue background
represents the Māori navigators who resulted in the Māori settlement of New Zealand
all those hundreds of years ago. No flag could better reflect the Treaty of Waitangi
partnership. No flag could better represent that partnership.
By contrast, John Key originally wanted a black flag, but he then realised the
connection that that would have with the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria and he
suddenly went quiet about that. And, in any event, a black flag is much too funereal. He
also wanted a silver fern, but that confuses a sports symbol —as Jono Naylor did in his
speech—with the needs of a national flag. They are two totally different things. The flag
needs to represent the partnership between the two cultures: the British heritage, and the
Pacific and Māori culture. That is New Zealand, that represents New Zealand, and that
is the way it should stay. John Key wants to sell out all of that and the current flag
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5351
without thinking it through, without any genuine public support, and without regard to
the damage that it will do to New Zealand’s interests and heritage.
On that matter, the current flag has a good reputation where it matters in the world:
in the UK, in the Commonwealth, in sporting events, in the United Nations, and so on.
We benefit from the prestige that that flag gives us, of having a British and a Pacific and
Māori culture, and it could not represent that better. We will gain little or nothing by
having an unknown new flag, which would take decades even to be recognised in
overseas places—or even in New Zealand, for that matter.
There is also another very important reason for us to oppose this bill for a new flag,
and it is that it will betray the men who fought and died under that flag in many world
wars and in other wars. The respect that the current flag generates, from having flown
everywhere where our men have fought, should never be disregarded in the cavalier
way that the National Government is doing with this awful bill. Why would we want to
lose that heritage, that history, and that connection? And, make no mistake, they will be
lost if a new flag is adopted. They will be lost —that is the truth. In clause 69 the bill
purports to preserve the current flag, as depicted in new schedule 1A, but only as a flag
of “historical significance”. What a terrible way to treat our New Zealand flag. It will
not really be preserved at all. It would actually be relegated to history, and, as such, that
would be something of an insult, I believe, to all of the people who fell defending that
flag and this country in two world wars.
This is not an honest or a respectf ul way to treat that flag. There is absolutely no
reason whatsoever for a new flag, and nobody has yet described to me in a way that I
can understand or appreciate why the flag has to be changed at all. Some members
opposite have talked about the future and about having a progressive nation. Are they
saying that the current New Zealand flag cannot represent a forward -looking and
progressive nation? It has so far —it has so far. Why would it not in the future? There is
no genuine or significant public pressur e for a change of the flag. There is public
pressure for genuine constitutional reform —Māori seats, a written constitution, the size
of Parliament, the length of the parliamentary term, the Māori electorate option and
participation, the role of the Treaty of Waitangi, and so on. So what do we do? We have
a referendum on one thing only —the least important thing of the lot: the flag. What
about all of those other things? Why are they not part of this referendum? Why are the
things that will actually make a difference not being referred to the New Zealand public
by way of a referendum? For all of these reasons, New Zealand First will continue to
lead the campaign against this bad legislation, its flawed process, and any suggestion
that this country needs a new flag.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Kia ora, e te Mana Whakawā,
tēnā koe e te Whāre. Ko tēnei Te Wiki o Te Reo Māori me whakanuia e tātau!
[Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker, greetings to you the House. This is Māori Language
Week and we must celebrate it!]
I am delighted that we are having this debate today, and I am fervently hoping that it
will lead to a new national flag that is not constantly confused with Australia’s, but
around which we as New Zealanders can proudly unite. It is not just because I want
change for the sake of change—far from it. For me it is very personal, and, in many
respects, it relates directly to arguments that have just been put by Mr O’Rourke, which
I completely refute. It is because the emblem that New Zealanders unite under, and,
most important, that is on both moving and very numerous New Zealand headstones
and tombstones throughout the battlefields of Western Europe, is not the New Zealand
flag; it is the silver fern.

items.speaker: Darroch Ball
items.text: Why are you changing it now?
5352 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I will come to that as well. I never met my maternal great -
grandfather, Hugh Francis Wright, but I know three things about him. The first is that
my mother loved him and admired him. The second is that he was, in his day, one of
New Zealand’s leading mountaineers, which I have to say is a talent he certainly did not
pass on to this particular great -grandson. And the third is that at the outbreak of Wor ld
War I he was considered too old to enlist, and so even though he offered to do so he was
declined on the grounds of age. But then, after the devastating losses in Western Europe
throughout 1914, 1915, and 1916, there was a new wave of enlisters, and older men
were accepted for enlistment, and my great -grandfather was one of them. He went and
fought in the First World War, and, I am pleased to say, returned to New Zealand at the
end of it.
I did not know my paternal grandfather, Charles Grierson Macindoe, and, at the other
end of the age bracket, legend has it that he lied about his age and ran away at the start
of the Boer War, and he served there. This year on Anzac Day for the first time I
proudly wore his medals on my right lapel, something I had neve r felt I could do before
but I was very proud to do. I did, of course, know my father, and my father served in the
Second World War. He was an Aircrew Allocation Centre instructor, and, along with
his brother, he served in the Pacific, he was injured in an accident there, and his brother
carried on to Europe. My uncle, whom I never met, Raymond Kenneth Grierson
Macindoe, was killed in action just a fortnight before the end of the war —just before
VE-Day. The war was virtually over, and he is buried in Forli in southern Italy where he
fell, and the silver fern is the emblem that identifies him as a New Zealander.
So for me this is very personal, and for me the timing is absolutely right to be
making the change in this year as we honour the legacy of all of those who have served
our country in the major conflicts through to the present day, because it is the silver fern
that is the emblem that they fought and died under and that honours their legacy. So I
utterly reject the argument that changing the flag in th is year is disrespectful. Mr
Mallard said it is wrong; the timing is wrong. I say: what finer way could we find to
honour the legacy of those courageous New Zealanders than to honour their
contribution with a change of the flag of the type I have said? So not just any change,
but a flag that shows what we have in common.
The Union Jack reflects my heritage. Obviously, with a name like Macindoe, I have
Scottish ancestry, but I believe it is totally incongruous here in the 21st century for us, as
a proud and  independent nation, to still have another country’s flag on our flag. The
New Zealand First Party has argued against the cost of this exercise. I say to them: what
cost is democracy? It may not cost as much as $26 million, but put it in the context of
our annual expenditure, which is in the region of $73 billion. A referendum is the best
way and the fairest way to consult all New Zealanders and to give them their say, and I
am proud that we are doing it.
This is the same process, to those who argue against it, that New Zealanders
followed about 20 years ago when we changed our electoral system from first past the
post to MMP. Those members who now object so strongly to what we are doing would
not be here i f we had not had that exercise, and they should reflect on that. Would
Canada go back to its flag of pre -1965? Of course it would not. It is very proud of its
maple leaf, and wherever you go around the world if you see someone wearing
something with the ma ple leaf, you know either that they are Canadian or they have
recently visited that country. I want the same for New Zealanders.
I do not want us to be constantly confused with Australians and, in many cases,
others, and I am utterly appalled by the disingenuousness and, frankly, the blatant
dishonesty, particularly of the Labour Party, which now wants to pretend to this nation
that it is opposed to this process when its own 2014 election policy it said: “Labour will:
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5353
… review the design of the New Zealand  flag involving flag design experts and with
full public consultation and involvement.” “We believe that the time has come …”, said
Labour, “and it is right for the issue to be put to the public.” And what did Mr Andrew

items.speaker: Little say when asked
items.text: “Should NZ ch ange its flag: What’s your personal opinion?
Should there be a referendum?” Mr Little said: “I think a referendum is a suitable way
to deal with an issue that can be very polarising.”
What absolute claptrap and disingenuous behaviour from Labour members now —to
resile from that position purely for populist reasons. There is no principle in their
argument at all, and they know it. That is why their heads are down. They know that
they want it, and, as the Prime Minister and Bill English have both said, the onl y reason
they do not support us in this debate is that we are doing it. If they were doing it, they
would be leading the charge and we would be supporting them. If New Zealanders
reflect on this issue, and I hope they will, and decide to retain our current  flag, then I
will respect their opinion, but I hope that they will think about it seriously. And, more
important, I have to say I would be very disappointed at such a lost opportunity, which
we will not enjoy again in our lifetime, and members should refl ect on that. We will not
have this opportunity again in our lifetime if we do not seize it this time around.
If the flag review panel —and I want to commend the members on the outstanding
work that they have been doing —provides an attractive option that includes the silver
fern, for the reasons that I have already outlined, I shall proudly vote for that option,
particularly to honour the legacy of our forebears including my own relatives about
whom I spoke earlier in this debate.
I am happy to accept the invitations that the New Zealand First Party members have
challenged me to accept, to go to the RSAs to meet wi th veterans and to have this
discussion with them, because I will prove to them that I honour their legacy, that I do
respect them, that I share and understand and value all of the things that they stand for,
and, that I want to acknowledge their sacrifice  and their service with the change that we
are debating today. I respect those who hold a contrary view because of their great
passion for the current New Zealand flag, but I utterly reject any suggestion that this is
the wrong time to consider changing it. On the contrary, this is the ideal time to honour
the outstanding service of men and women who have served our nation. This is the ideal
time to say we can have something about which we feel proud, and there is an emblem
that we proudly wear when we go t o sporting events, that we proudly see on New
Zealanders who travel abroad, and, in a very sombre and moving way, that we see as we
move up and down the rows and rows of those war cemeteries of Western Europe.
So I want to honour the legacy of Hugh Franci s Wright, of Charles Grierson
Macindoe, of Harley Lieman Grierson Macindoe, and, in particular, my Uncle Ken,
whom I never met, by making this change. I cannot more strongly commend this bill to
the House.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A 5-minute call from the Green Party.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: E Te Ūpoko o Te Paopao a Piringa tēnā koe.
[Mr Speaker of the House of Idle Talk, greetings to you.]
What we are debating today is actually a symbol. A flag is a very powerful and very
important symbol. It is a symbol of a nation State, a symbol of a political identity, and,
to a lesser extent perhaps, a symbol of a shared cultural identity. It is important. This
symbol has already tr iggered one shooting war in New Zealand. If you recall our
history, our northern tupuna Hone Heke took exception to the fact that the symbol of
British power was being flown above Kororāreka rather than the flag of New Zealand,
which 10 years earlier had been acknowledged by the British monarchy and by the
Admiralty. One hopes that this debate currently will not come to blows, but,
nevertheless, it is a critically important conversation we are having about this symbol.
5354 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
I guess our objection to this bill is  that, in my view —and it is a common enough
phrase—form should follow function. Of course, that comes from architecture —that the
purpose of a building should drive its design. In this instance, the function is our
constitutional arrangements that underpin our political identity; the form is the symbol
that we fly to represent our nation State, which is, of course, a flag. We are having this
debate and a referendum —$26 million of expenditure —worrying about changing the
form, when we should be addressing the function, which is the underlying constitutional
arrangements.
It is true that in 2010 the Government did establish a panel, the independent
Constitutional Advisory Panel, which in 2013 reported back with its findings. With all
due respect to the eminent New Zealanders who sat on the panel, their recommendation,
which was perhaps a little underwhelming, was that we should continue the
conversation. It was a very genuine and a thoughtful enough recommendation, and a
very real one.
It is fair to say that th is current flag consultation process has struggled to get the
numbers. We have all seen the pictures of halls prepared for 100 people, with five or six
embarrassed-looking people and probably a larger number of officials.
The Constitutional Advisory Panel back in 2010, or thereabouts, received something
like 5,259 submissions, which, in the words of Mr English—who spoke earlier today —
indicated some interest in the nation’s constitutional framework. Mr English then went
on to say: “although there is no sense of an urgent or widespread desire for change”. So,
by Mr English’s admission in 2013, New Zealanders are not jumping up and down in
the street for this. I think there is a groundswell and a feeling that we need to look hard
at our constitution and, there fore, at the symbols that represent us as a nation State, but
there seems to not be the urgency. It seems peculiar that we are spending an inordinate
amount of time and a remarkable amount of money debating the form, rather than the
function, of our constitution.
I think we would not need to spend $26 million to think hard and to perhaps develop
a new, more fit for purpose constitution. We have a very good model, a matika mai,
which is a project being led by Moana Jackson, a lawyer specialising in constitutional
and Māori and te Tiriti issues particularly, who, along with a very well -informed
powerful team of people, and for very little money, continues to go around the country
talking about what our constitution could look like.
I think it is fair to say that too often the question posed is: how might Te Tiriti o
Waitangi fit into our constitutional arrangements? That is the wrong question. The
question we need to ask is what form of constitutional arrangement logically emerges
from our Te Tiriti o Waitang i, which, I think, we collectively recognise as the founding
document of our country. That is the debate we should be having, rather than this rather
tangential debate about the symbolism, about the flag —about what has been described
as the piece of coloured cloth. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Karanga ahau a Marama Fox, tēnā koe. A 5-minute call.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: Tēnā koe, e te Mana Whakawā me
tō kaha ki te whakahua i tō tātau Reo Māori. Ā, he Reo Māori taku kōrero. Ā, tēnā
koutou e te Whare, nei te mihi atu ki a tātau katoa, tēnā koe, tēnā koutou, ā, nei te mihi
atu ki te Whare.
Ā, āe tika rā te kōrero, he āhua t aumaha tēnei i runga i te pokohiwi o Te Iwi Māori
me te whenua—te pōharatanga, te pani, me te rawakore. Ā, kua rongona mātau ki taua
kōrero: “He moumou pūtea tēnei kōrero mō te haki.” Āe, kai te whakaae au ki tēnā, kei
te whakaae au ki tēnā. Heoi anō, kai te whakapaua taua pūtea, ahakoa tō mātau
whakaae. Nā reira ki au nei, me mau tēnei take kia tutuki pai tēnei kōrero kai mua i te
aroaro o te whatu.
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5355
I ahau e huri rauna i te motu, kai te kōrero au ki aku hoa, ki aku whanaunga, ā, ki ngā
marae o te motu, ki  ngā kuia, ki ngā koroua, ki ngā kaumātua. Kāre rātau i te kite i Te
Iwi Māori i roto i tēnei haki o Aotearoa e rere nei i tēnei wā. Kāre rātau i te kite i te
kaha o Te Iwi Māori kai roto i tēnei haki, o tēnei wā. Nā reira, i whakaae au kia tīnihia
tēnei haki. Kai te hiahia au kia rapua tētahi tohu, e whakamārama ana i ngā taha e rua o
te whenua nei: kia kitea Te Māoritanga i roto i te haki; te haki e tū nei ki runga i ngā
Whare Pāremata, te haki e tū nei ki runga i te pokohiwi o te tangata e oma haere ana mō
Aotearoa. Kai te pīrangi au ki te kite i Te Iwi Māori i roto.
I rongo au i te kōrero o tēnei o te mema, Denis O’Rourke, e kī nei, āe, ēnei whetū,
me tēnei tae kahurangi nei hai whakahua, ko Te Iwi Māori tenei. Mehemea e whakaae
ana mātau ki tēnā, he aha te take ka hiahia mātau i tō mātau ake haki? He aha te take, ka
whakairia te iwi o Ngāpuhi, o Ngāti Hine, i te haki o Te Whakapuakitanga? Ā, ko te
take, kāre rātau i kite i a rātau anō i roto i tēnei haki o Aotearoa.
I kī mai ētahi, i mate ō tātau tūpun a i runga i ngā whīra pakanga o te ao i raro i te
haki, i whawhai mō te haki. Kai te whakahē au i taua kōrero. Kāre rātau i whawhai mō
te haki, i whawhai rātau mō te toto, mō te whakapapa, mō ā rātau hoa, mō ngā hōia kai ā
rātau taha, mō ā rātau whānau, mō  ā rātau marae. Koirā te take e whawhai ana. Kāre
rātau e whawhai mō tēnei haki. Kai raro i tēnei haki haere atu Te Hokowhitu -ā-Tū ki
ngā pakanga o te ao. Kāre tēnei Kāwana me te haki nei i hoatu i te pū ki a rātau.
Karekau! I hoatu kē i tētahi spade, kāre au i te mōhio i te kupu mō te “spade”, hai keri i
te whenua, kia hono ai te tangata. Kāre rātau i whakatakoto i tō rātau kaha i runga i ngā
pakanga o te ao mō te haki.
I a rātau e hoki mai ana ki Aotearoa nei, kāore tonu tēnei haki, tēnei Kāwana, i
whakamana i a rātau, i a rātau i hoki atu ki tō rātau whenua. Kāre rātau i whiwhi pūtea,
kāre rātau i whiwhi whenua. I tangohia kētia te whenua o Te Māori i a rātau e hoki atu
ana ki te kāinga, kai raro i tēnei haki.
Nā reira, e kī atu ana au, kāre au i whakaae ki tēnei haki. Kai te pīrangi au kia tīnihia,
kia kite whānui tātau katoa, kai roto i tō tātau tohu, Māori, tauiwi, ki raro i te haki
kotahi. Āe, tika rā te kōrero—maha kē atu ngā take kai mua i a tātau, ā, ngā pūtake ō
tātau, āe, kia tutuki pai. Heoi anō he tīmatanga noa tēnei. Tīmata ki te haki, whai atu ki
te waiata o Aotearoa nei, whai tonutia ki te ture ki raro i Te Tiriti o Waitangi—kia
whakamanahia ki roto i Te Ture. Ā, koinei tāku, he tīmatanga noa ka pā atu nei Te Iwi
Māori me te iwi tauiwi. Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā mai tātau katoa.
[Greetings and congratulations to you, Mr Deputy Speaker, in your efforts to speak
our Māori language. My address will be in Māori as a consequence. So greetings to you
collectively, the House. I commend us all: you, Mr Deputy Speaker, and, indeed,
everyone present here—well done, the House.
Yes, the statement —the poor, the orphaned, and the underprivileged— is a fair one,
and somewhat of a burden upon the shoulder of Māoridom and the country. We have
heard the comment: “This talk about the flag is a waste of funding.” Yes, I agree with
that quite emphatically. None the less, that funding is being spent, even though we agree
it is a waste of money. And so, to me, we progress this matter so that this consultation
before us is completed well.
So as I went around the country I was talking with my friends, relatives, marae
around the country, elderly women and men folk, and the aged. They are not seeing
Māoridom in this flag of New Zealand that is flying currently. The y are not seeing the
intensity of Māoridom in this current flag. Hence, I agree that this flag be changed and
I want a search to be undertaken for a symbol that will reflect both sides of this country
so that its Māoritanga is seen clearly in the flag: in the flag flying on the Houses of
Parliament, the flag on the shoulders of an athlete running for New Zealand. I want to
see Māoridom in it.
5356 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
I heard that member Denis O’Rourke’s address. Yes, the member said, these stars,
this blue colour to announce that this is Māoridom. If we agree to that, why would we
want our own flag? Why would the Ngāpuhi tribe and the Ngāti Hine tribe fly the flag of
the Declaration of Independence? The reason is that they do not really see themselves
in this New Zealand flag.
Others said to me that our ancestors died on the battlefields of the world fighting
under the flag. They fought for the flag. I reject that asse rtion. They did not fight for the
flag; they fought for blood, genealogy and their mates, the soldiers by their sides, their
families and marae. That is the reason why they were fighting. They were not fighting
for this flag. The Māori Battalion went to th e world wars under this flag. This
Government and flag did not arm them. No! They gave them a spade instead— I do not
know what the Māori word is for “spade” —to dig trenches so a person can link up.
They did not exert themselves on the battlefields of the world for the flag.
As they came back here to New Zealand, this flag and Government did not empower
them as they went back to their own part of the country. They did not receive any
funding, any land. Under this flag, Māori land was being taken instead as they were
going back home.
Therefore, I am telling you that I am not in favour of this flag. I want it changed so
that we can all see broadly that our symbol contains a Māori and non- Māori
perspective in it under the one flag. Yes, the assertion is correc t—there are many other
issues before us, yes, our very own issues that we need to address to achieve a
satisfactory outcome. But this is simply the beginning. The flag is just the beginning.
The national anthem follows next, and immediately afterwards the Treaty of Waitangi
given effect under the Act. Yes, from me personally, it is merely a beginning that will
impact upon Māori and non- Māori. I commend, acknowledge, and applaud you and us
all collectively, thank you.]

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Tēnā koe e Minita o Te Wiki o Te Reo Māori. It is
an honour to be able to speak in the second reading on this bill, the New Zealand Flag
Referendums Bill. I have to be honest. When this thought —this idea about us heading
towards a referendum, and even the changing of the flag —initially came out, my first
impression was to ask what the reason was. What was the purpose, and what was the
sense in us heading in this direction?
I then began to reflect that in 2012 and 2013 there was a consultation process in
regard to the constitution, or the forming of a constitution—just as has been spoken
about by the previous speaker, Marama Fox, and other speakers—and about the place of
Te Tiriti o Waitangi and other aspects of what  defines us as a nation. In some of those
consultations there was a discussion by some people about the national anthem and the
things that constitute national identity. There was an issue that was raised by some
about the flag, as well as other areas. So the constitution discussion actually began to
bring up this question about what defines us as a nation.
Then, in going through this process, I began to look into where this began—this
whole idea around the call for a New Zealand flag. Well, this happened over 40 years
ago. I want to just mention this because there is a thought out there in the public and in
the nation that this is simply an idea by our Prime Minister, the Rt Hon John Key —that
he has just thought this up as a great idea. In fact, this has been happening over many
decades previously. So let me just give us an idea about where this has come from.
There have been numerous calls in the last four decades for a new flag to be adopted.

items.speaker: Darroch Ball
items.text: Citizens started that last one, Alfred, not the Government —citizens
did.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: So if Mr Ball listens, he will maybe have just a little bit of
education here. In 1970 National MP and the Minister of Internal Affairs, Allan Highet,
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5357
also put forward the idea. He asked: does this flag not only represent our history and
heritage but is it a reflection of our future? That idea was actually removed—it did not
have the traction. In 1988 Labour MP and the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Russel l
Marshall, also put forward the idea. The thought about this fact was that, again, here is
the flag—around the idea of national identity and nationhood, should we be reflecting
on the idea of having a new flag?
In 1989 the Listener  magazine ran a competi tion for designs. There were over 600
entries and seven finalists, including the current flag, the 1902 flag, and what was
surprising is that that flag won by only just a small majority —a very small majority.
Here is what Gordon Campbell, who was the editor of the Listener  at that time and who
ran the competition, said. He said that despite the result, it was confirmed that it had
exploded the myths about New Zealanders’ devotion to the flag.
In February 1992 the late Hon Matiu Rata, a former Minister of M āori Affairs and
the founder of Mana Motuhake, called for a redesign to re -establish a national identity.
He called for a redesign to be able to look at this, and here was his point of difference.
He asked whether, even in this House, this current flag represents our history and our
heritage. We have heard arguments today that, yes, it does. But then he said this: “But
does it represent our future, heading into a bicultural nation?”.
At that time, the RSA had a petition from over 10,000 signatories who argued, again,
that they did not want to change the flag. Over several of these attempts, the RSA came
to the point where it said that it realised that, unlike with the previous three attempts, if
this decision was to be made, then the decision to change the flag should be done via a
referendum—it should be done via a referendum. So what are we doing at the moment?
We are actually talking about a bill that is about having a referendum as well.
In 1998 Marie Hasler, the Minister of Cultural Affairs, also talke d about and argued
in favour of the existing flag, but said she would support a change if it was shown that
the will of the people was there for a referendum. This has been going on. In 2004
Wellington businessman Lloyd Morrison formed a trust called the N ZFlag.com Trust.
The purpose was, again, to ask whether we should be changing the flag and whether
there should be a referendum. There were supporters like Cath Tizard, Keith Quinn,
Susan Devoy —a number of them there. We know that they were not able to get  a
referendum as they did not have enough signatories, but what I want to say is that the
point I am making out of this is that this issue has been going on for a long time. The
idea of changing the flag in regard to reflecting our history and our heritage  and, most
important, our future, has been going on for a long time.
We have heard speeches in the House that have clearly said this. From the Greens,
Russel Norman supports changing the flag. He may not like the process, but he would
support a change, as  would others, in regard to our constitution. We know that on the
other side the Hon Trevor Mallard came to our select committee. He even indicated that
he would support a change to the flag. However, what he did not like was the process.
We know that acr oss the House the majority of members, bar New Zealand First,
support the change to the flag. The truth of the reality is that members on the other side
will not support it because those members —who are supposedly the nation- builders of
the country in desc ribing this identity —are not the ones who are in control of this
process. That is the reason why we are heading towards this.
I just want to come to a couple of other points. There were some points that we were
talking about. People also know that we have a Māori flag. It is the flag that is flown on
Waitangi Day, and the name is just escaping me at the moment. Peeni, you might be
able to help me there—

items.speaker: Peeni Henare
items.text: Tino Rangatiratanga.
5358 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: The Tino Rangatiratanga flag, thank you. That is flown and has
been acknowledged and recognised. The Government allowed for that initiative to be
able to happen so that there could be the opportunity for that flag to be flown. So I want
to just rebut some of the comments by Denis  O’Rourke when he said that even Māori
support this current flag. I suggest that those comments are not true. I suggest those
comments would be rebutted, even by other speakers. This flag was not chosen by
referendum, nor by Māori. I would suggest that the re are others, like Matiu Rata, who
would say that this current flag of 1902 does not reflect our future —it does not reflect
our future.
In 1989 the Government also approved—let us talk about the cost. People have been
talking about this cost of $26 million. Look, we know that the timing of that is quite
challenging, but in 1989 the Government took the time to acknowledge the fact that
1990 was the sesquicentennial year of the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi —$20
million was put aside to acknowledge that. Why? Because it was important in the
building and the acknowledging and the shaping of a nation. So we think that is really
important.
In fact, when we think about the submitters, there were only 113 of those submitters
who considered the referendum process to be too expensive. The Government considers
that to have a process that is legitimate and democratic and for the outcome to endure, it
is important to do it properly, and that is to do it via a referendum. We have heard again
that this is so that the  nation may choose —not the Government, but the nation may
choose.
I just want to make a couple of comments from the Hon Trevor Mallard. He named
the National Party members on the Justice and Electoral Committee and talked about
the democratic process of h aving oral submissions—in fact, he talked about there being
740 oral submissions. It is true to say that those came in as form submissions. It is
standard process and protocol that those form submissions, whatever form they take, are
often collated to be one submission before the select committee, so we did not believe
that we were denying any rights whatsoever for others to be able to do that.
There were many submitters who had actually submitted and actually took the
time—in fact, there were 259 submissi ons, of which 27 submitters chose to make an
oral submission. It would not have taken much for those 740 people to have written
something quite different —not a form submission—to indicate their right and their
willingness to come and submit before the comm ittee. They did not do that. It was a
form submission.
I just want to finish on the last comments that I think are really important. There was
a comment, again by the Hon Trevor Mallard, about how in the cross -party group there
was unanimous agreement—bar the Government members at that time—towards having
one referendum. That was contested. I can say that that was contested. Even from the
Māori Party, those members had agreed, and do agree, with the process that the
Government is taking. It is wrong to ind icate that it was only the Government members
who were willing to take this process of having two referendums. We believe that this
process is important.
I look forward to the Committee of the whole House stage. But, most important, I
actually look forward to the process of going out into those RSAs, as I have been— I am
a member of Te Atatū RSA —and to be able to talk continually about the importance
and the role that this referendum has in the shaping of our nation and the changing,
potentially, of the flag. Whatever the nation chooses, at the end of the day, it is what we
will all also abide by. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: PEENI HENARE
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Māngai o te
Whare, otirā, tēnā tātau katoa ki roto i tēnei tūāhuatanga, arā ko Te Wiki o Te Reo
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5359
Māori, kei te pātaitia e tēnei Whare te mana o te tangata ki tētahi haki. Koinā tāku e mea
atu ana, koia rā tērā ko te pai o Te Reo Māori. Anā, he  aha nei nakena ngā haki tūturu o
te whenua nei? Ko Te Reo tēnā i tupu mai i te whenua, koinā tāku e kōrero atu ana ahau
ki a tātau, tēnā tātau katoa.
Ka tīkina ake ahau ngā kōrero a te mema ki tērā taha o te Whare, Alfred  Ngaro, e
kōrero ana mō te ture Kāwanatanga constitution. Anā, i tīmataria ai e tēnei
Kāwanatanga te mahi kia whiwhi ai i ngā whakaaro o te motu whānui mō tēnei mea te
ture Kāwanatanga. Anā, i roto i ngā whakaputanga o taua Rōpū Whiriwhiri Take e pā
ana ki te ture Kāwanatanga, kīhei rātou i mea atu, me tīni te haki nei. Koinā tāku e mea
atu ana, kei te whai tēnei Kāwanatanga i tō rātou ake whiore. Koinā te take, kei te kūiti
tēnei Kāwanatanga i te motu whānui. E kūiti ana tēnei Kāwanatanga i roto i tētahi
kūititanga, ki te mea atu, mehemea e hiahia ana koutou ki te tīnihia i te haki, tēnā, anei
hoki ko ngā whiriwhiringa kei mua i a koutou. Ēngari, ko tā mātou e mea atu ana, me
tukuna te pātai tika i te tuatahi. He aha nei nakena ki te pātai tika, anā. Mehemea e
hiahia ana te motu whānui kia tīnihia te haki, koinā hoki ko te pātai tuatahi, ki a au nei.
Ka whakaaro ake ahau ki wētahi o ngā kōrero ka puta mai i te rangi nei e pā ana ki te
taha pūtea. E mōhio ana tātou katoa, ko te tini o te pūtea ka whakapauhia  ki runga i
tēnei take. He mea moumou. Nui ake ngā take kei mua i te aroaro o tēnei motu whānui,
arā, te pōharatanga, te mātauranga, he tini. Koinei tāku atu ki te Kāwanatanga i tēnei
tāima. Mehemea e ngākaunui ana ngā hunga nei ki ngā RSAs, tēnā, hoatu te pūtea ki
ngā RSAs tā te mea, mōhio ana tātou kei te hinga haere te rahi o te pūtea ki aua wāhi
rā—he wāhi maumaharatanga mō ngā hōia. Kāti!
Ka whakaaro ake ahau ki ngā kōrero o te mema o tērā taha o te Whare, Alfred Ngaro.
Hei tāna, ko te mana o te hōia ki roto i ngā pakanga kua pahure ake nei. Ka whakaaro
ake ahau mō tōku tupuna a Te Hāringi, Te Hāringi Rīwhi. I whawhai te kaumātua rā ki
roto i Te Pakanga Tuatahi o te Ao, ki roto hoki i Te Pakanga Tuarua o te Ao. I te ata ka
āra mai a Te Hāringi ki raro i te maru o tō tātou haki. I te mutunga o te rā, kīhai a Te
Hāringi i hoki mai ki te kāinga. Anā, ka mate ki raro tonu i te maru o taua haki. Ko te
mate kē, kīhai ōna hoa hōia i kimi i tōna tūpāpaku. Nō reira, ka takoto ake a Hāri ki roto
o wāhi kē. Ēngari  i te mutunga o te rā, ka tuohu te mātenga o ōna hoa hōia ki te haki e
hāwhe kake nei ki runga i te pou haki. Nō reira, koia rā wētahi o tāku e mea atu ana, i
whawhai ngā mātua, ngā tūpuna mō te haki te take. E mea atu ana, ā, e kāhore! Ko Te
Kīngi, ko te whenua o te mana motuhake. Ēngari e mea atu ana ahau, i haere rātou ki
raro i te maru o te haki, i hoki anō mai rātou i raro i taua haki.
Nō reira kāti! Ka whakaaro ake ahau mō ētahi atu o ngā take, ko te take nui ahakoa te
aha, mōhio ana tātou ko te whakapautanga o te pūtea mō te kore take noa iho. Tukuna te
pātai tika i te tuatahi, mai i te tīmatanga o tēnei kaupapa, ā, kāti, ka tahuri atu ahau ki
roto i te reo tuarua hei whakakapi ake i tōku kōrero i te rā nei.
[Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker, and at the same time I extend my greetings to us all
in the circumstances of this, Māori Language Week. This House questions the integrity
of an individual against that of a flag, and that is the reason why I have said to you
collectively that the Māori language is s o appealing. Now then, what is there about the
flags of this country that is so indigenous? On the other hand the Māori language
evolved from the land, and that is the real reason why I am addressing us in Māori, so
hello there to us all.
I take up the sentiments of the member on that side of the House, Alfred Ngaro, about
the Government’s action relating to the constitution. Now then, this Government
instigated a process to obtain the views of the nation at large about it. Now, that
Constitutional Advisor y Panel never stated in its releases that the flag of this nation
must be changed. And that is why I am saying to you: this Government is chasing its
own tail. That is the reason this Government is putting a squeeze on the nation at large.
5360 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015

items.speaker: It is narrowing the confinement and saying
items.text: well then, here are the options as well in
front of you. But we are saying to Government, release the proper question first. But
what, indeed, is the proper question? That is it! Now if the nation desires a change that,
in fact, to me is the first question.
I ponder over some of the comments relating to funding that emerged today. We are
all aware that an enormous amount of funding will be spent on this matter. It is sheer
waste of funding. There are so many other issues confronting the nation, like poverty,
education—myriads. At this very moment, this is mine to Government. If these ones in
Government are committed to RSAs, well then, give the funding to RSAs, because we
are all aware that funding in places like those—memorial places for armed forces.
Enough! I reflect on the sentiments of the member on that side of the House, Alfred
Ngaro. To that member the status of the soldier in battle has passed. I reflect on my
ancestor Te Hāringi, Te Hāringi Rīwhi, that elderly one who f ought in the First World
War, and in the Second World War, as well. In the morning Te Hāringi woke up from
under the shelter of our flag. At day’s end Te Hāringi did not come home. He died there
under the shelter of the flag. The real misfortune was that his comrades did not look for
his body. So Hāri was interred somewhere else. But at day’s end his fellow soldiers
bowed their heads to the flag flying at half mast on the flag pole. So those are some of
my reflections that I am alluding to about parents and ancestors fighting for the flag. It
is asserting: no! It was for the King and independence of the country. But I do assert
that they went under the shelter of the flag, and they returned, as well, under that flag.
And so enough. I can think of other matt ers, but the most significant one, above all
else, is our awareness that funding is being spent for no reason at all. Release the
proper question first from the outset of this proposal. Well now, to conclude my address
today I turn to the second language.]
In conclusion, it seems pretty set from the Government that this change is going to
happen despite the call of this nation that now is not the right time. So if it is going to
happen it seems that the only way that this flag will rise up the flagpole and also
continue to blow proudly in the sky is on the hot air coming from the other side of the
House. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I think it says everything about the
current Government’s priorities that at a time when the economy is in serious difficulty,
when there are riots at privatised prisons, when charter schools are falling over, and
when the Government is hocking off State houses and literally driving pensioners out of
their homes —literally driving pensioners out of their homes —it wants to devote the
time of this House to a referendum on the flag. And it is not just the time of the House it
is using in this referendum process; it is also $26 million of taxpayers’ mone y. That
says everything about the current Government’s priorities.
John Key went on television a couple of weeks ago and said: “I, as Prime Minister,
want overt signs of patriotism.” That is his goal —overt signs of patriotism. Well, my
message for John Ke y is quite simple. If he wants New Zealanders to be more patriotic
and more proud of their country he should give them something to be proud of. A flag is
a symbol, but, actually, what Governments do is far more important.
There have been moments when New  Zealand Prime Ministers on both sides of the
House have inspired New Zealanders to be proud of their country. David Lange stood
up at the Oxford Union debate and, regardless of what flag it was under, he made New
Zealanders proud to be New Zealanders. Whe n Helen Clark stood up and took in the
Tampa boat people she made New Zealanders proud to be New Zealanders. I have got
to say, as a New Zealander, that I was proud of New Zealand when Jim Bolger and
Doug Graham and those other people on the National Party side were leading the Treaty
settlements process. That made me proud to be a New Zealander. That was not
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5361
involving a flag; that was involving genuine action by the Government that made New
Zealanders proud.
So my message to John Key is that if he wants N ew Zealanders to be more patriotic
and proud of their country, he should give them something to be proud of. And it is not
going to be kicking pensioners out of their State houses like this Government is doing.
It is not going to be turning the other way w hen our primary producing industries
struggle in the current economy, which the National Government is turning a blind eye
to. Those things are not going to make New Zealanders proud, and a simple referendum
on a change of flag is not going to make New Zealanders proud at the moment, not at a
time when there are so many other things New Zealanders are worried about.
I have been very clear all along. I would like to see a flag that better reflects the New
Zealand that we are today and the New Zealand that w e will be in the future. I have
been very clear about that—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Support the bill.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: —and I have got to say to Nick Smith that it is one of the
reasons I do not want a referendum that is doomed to fail. What the referendum will do
is actually take the whole issue away for generations. We will not get to discuss this
again when this refer endum is voted down, and it is doomed to be voted down because
of the mismanagement of this National Government.
Let us be clear about how badly this issue is going for the Government. How many
people showed up at public meetings? Just 700 people showed up at the meetings that
the Government has been having around the country —739 members of the public. That
is $550 per person just for the cost of the meetings. But if you add in the amount of
money the Government spent advertising the meetings as well, it i s over $2,000 per
person who showed up at those meetings at a time when New Zealanders have much
more important priorities on their mind. The Government sent out 1.6 million postcards.
Only 15,000 of those were returned. That is $93 per postcard returned. That is the cost
that we are talking about. These are not trivial sums of money at a time when there are
so many other things that New Zealanders want to their Government to be spending
money on. But, of course, New Zealanders have come to accept waste as part and parcel
of this Government.
Finally, I want to talk to Tim Macindoe, who gave a very good speech in this debate.
I want to commend him for his speech. He spoke about veterans of both world wars and
his relations who were veterans of both world war s. I say to him that I admire the
contribution he made to this debate, but if the Government is so concerned about
veterans and so interested in the views of veterans and what they fought for, why did it
give the RSA only 10 minutes at the Justice and Elec toral Committee? Why is the
Government willing to spend tens of millions of dollars on a referendum process when
it is not willing to spare more than 10 minutes for the RSA at the select committee? So
when National Government members show up to Anzac Day s ervices or World War I
commemorative services all around the country let them explain that to all the veterans
who are at those events. Let them explain why they think the RSA is so unimportant in
this process that they were willing to give it only 10 minu tes. This is not the time to be
doing this. This referendum is doomed to fail, and that is why the Government should
pull up stumps now.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: Let us put on the record for the House  the reason why
the Labour Party is opposed to this bill. It is spite —simple spite. That is the simple
reality of it. The Labour Party has this view of itself —this vainglorious view of itself—
that it is the party that does nationhood. It is the party of Norman Kirk at Waitangi. It is
the party of sending the ships over to Mururoa. It is the party of David Lange at the
Oxford Union giving that glorious speech. Look, I quoted David Lange in my maiden
5362 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 28 Jul 2015
speech. I agree that he was a great statesman, but the Labo ur Party does not have a
monopoly on nationhood, and it does not have a monopoly on taking New Zealand
forward.
Let us be very clear. The reason why the Labour Party is opposed to this bill is spite
and jealousy. They are jealous that it is a National -led Government, led by a Prime
Minister whom they despise, that is putting to the people the idea of changing the New
Zealand flag. They are jealous of it because it is Labour Party policy to have a
referendum on the flag. As late as September last year —in fact, as late as last week, on
its website—it was Labour Party policy to consider a flag referendum.
My good friend Charles Chauvel —the much -lamented Charles Chauvel —had a
member’s bill for a flag referendum in the ballot some time ago. The Labour Party is all
over this, except for the fact that it is a National Government doing it. It is really sad
because, actually, I reckon most Labour members agree with changing the flag. Andrew

items.speaker: Little certainly does. Last year he said
items.text: “My personal opinion is we should ha ve
something more relevant to an independent, small Asia -Pacific nation. I think a
referendum is a suitable way to deal with an issue that can be very polarising.” So the
Government, which took a policy of having a referendum to the election, and duly got
elected, has introduced legislation. And what do we have from the Labour Party today?
Well, it is going to oppose it. It is really, really sad.
New Zealand does not discuss nationhood and the issue of national identity enough,
in my view. This bill, and the process that we are undertaking, is part of that ongoing
conversation about what New Zealand is and what we should stand for. The question of
the flag is important. Yes, it is a just a symbol, but symbols matter —symbols matter.
The issue of whether, in t he 21st century, modern-day New Zealand is best represented
by a flag that has a Union Jack and the Southern Cross on it or whether we move to a
flag that better represents New Zealand’s national identity is an important one. We are
no longer a colony of G reat Britain. We are no longer tied by the apron strings to that
country—to the mother country. We have moved on from that, and the question as to
whether or not we should have a flag that better represents that new reality is something
that New Zealanders  are going to grapple with, and have been grappling with, during
this referendum process.
The process is important. We heard from Mr Chris Hipkins over there that New
Zealanders do not care about it, that they are totally unengaged, and that, to the extent
that they do care about the flag referendum process, they are absolutely opposed to
change. The ultimate referendum is the referendum that we are going to have. The
logical extension of the Labour Party’s argument on this stuff is that we should just
govern by opinion poll. It is that we should just put everything out to the people and
have a fleeting, cursory view of public opinion at one moment in time. No, actually, that
is not the right way to go about things. The right way to go about things, on an is sue as
important as this, is through a deliberative, consultative process in which people get a
chance to consider the issues widely and fully, have a say, and then get a vote on it.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: They have. They have, and t hey have given it the thumbs
down.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: It is not a New Zealand Herald online poll, Mr Cosgrove. It is not
some smidgen of public opinion at any one fixed point in time. It is through a
deliberative process, through a referendum. If  the Labour Party is correct, and if Mr
Hipkins is correct—he very rarely is on most other matters—and the people do not want
to change the flag, they will say so. This Government will respect that view —we will
respect that view. But if they vote for change, then the flag will change. The question
for the Labour Party is—after having exhausted all of this hot air arguing against giving
New Zealanders a say about the flag and the future of the flag in this country —will they
28 Jul 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5363
respect the outcome if people vote in favour of a change of flag? That is the question for
the Labour Party.
This referendum does not disrespect veterans. It does not do that. On the issue of
whether or not something is the right time, again, you could make that argument about
almost any change that the Government does. Well, it is never the right time. There has
not been a right time since 1970; there has not been the right time since 1980; it was not
the right time back in 2005, when hundreds of thousands of New Zealanders signed a
petition to change the flag. That is an argument for the status quo. It is a conservative
argument, and it is just hilarious that it is coming from the so-called progressive party of
social change over there —the party that likes to tell itself that it is all in favour of
moving New Zealand forward but that gives speech after speech saying: “It’s not the
right time. You know, we’re not sure New Zealanders are in favour of this.” They sound
like the conservative, fuddy -duddy party that the Labour Party has become. It is truly
tragic.
The Justice and Electoral Committee, which considered this bill, did a very good job
of considering the process. We considered the suggestion from Trevor Mallard and from
others that we should put a yes/no question in the first referendum that we are going to
have and that we are going to have quickly. Actually, we considered whether or not that
was a good idea, and we came to the view, by majority, that it was not a good idea. The
reason for that is, firstly, the Ministry of Jus tice officials recommended against it. The
reason is that it biases the referendum in favour of the status quo; it does not lead to a
mutual, objective referendum. In our view, that was not a good public policy outcome,
and that is why the majority of the select committee decided that the structure that we
have at the moment, which is the one recommended by the officials as being the most
neutral and objective referendum possible, is what we should do.
There were some suggestions that we should have a yes/no referendum to start
with—just put one question to the people: do you want to change the flag or not? The
problem with that, as somebody explained to me at a public meeting yesterday, is that
they may very well be in favour of changing the flag but that t hey just do not know
what it is going to change to, and until they have the options available, they are not sure.
That, with respect, is a silly suggestion by people who make it, including New Zealand
First. Denis O’Rourke, during the select committee proc ess, asked one question of all
the submitters, which was: why do we not just have a yes/no referendum question first?
I have just given the reason, for Denis’ benefit. The reason is that it is hard to make up
your mind whether or not you are in favour of c hange unless you know what you are
changing to. We decided to have the view that you should let people have a say on the
options first, and then it will be a binary, up or down vote on what the change will be.
We do not discuss constitutional questions enough in this House. We do not discuss
in this House issues of national identity. This is a good bill put forward by a good
Government. It is opposed by parties out of pure spite and jealousy.
The question was put that the amendments recommended by the Justice and Electoral
Committee be agreed to.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the question be agreed to.
Ayes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 58
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 12.
Question agreed to.

A party vote was called for on the question, That the New Zealand Flag Referendums
Bill be now read a second time.
Ayes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 58

Debate resumed from 21 July on the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill.
Environment Sector (continued)

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, when we were last progressing
the estimates debate we were debating the votes in the environment sector —volume
B.5, volume 3. They are Vote Conservation, Vote Environment, and Vote Parliamentary
Commissioner for the Environment. Scott Simpson had the call, and he has 2 minutes
and 20 seconds remaining, if he so wishes. Before giving the call to Mr Simpson, I
would like to remind the s elect committee chairs who are allocated calls, who lead the
sector debates, of the requirement of the Business Committee to set out the major
findings of their committees in relation to the estimates. Mr Simpson has set an
excellent example in this matter.
SCOTT SIMPSON (Chairperson of the Local Government and Environment
Committee): Mr Chairman, I appreciate the acknowledgment and also the opport unity
to conclude with a couple of minutes’ rounding out what, for me, is a very important
part of this Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill discussion and debate. It relates
exactly to the environmental sector, where two very competent Ministers preside  over
the most important environmental decisions and the stewardship of our precious
environment. Looking forward to the future, they are putting in place excellent
protections, excellent stewardship, and excellent advances that have not previously been
considered by other Governments.
In the field of conservation, the Minister of Conservation, Maggie Barry, is doing an
exceptional job. She is a person who has devoted her entire working life —not just in
this Parliament, but her entire working life —to ensur ing the advancement of
conservation matters and of our environment. In terms of the Minister for the
Environment, Nick Smith, he too has made a greater contribution—dare I say it —than
any other member in this House in terms of protecting and ensuring the e nhancement of
our natural environment.
I want to highlight one or two matters that came before the Local Government and
Environment Committee during the estimates hearings. I was particularly impressed
with the work that the Department of Conservation is doing in partnership agreements
with independent bodies and commercial organisations to leverage the funding and
access of resources for the further advancement and protection of our environment. I
particularly want to comment on, with appreciation, and note the work that Fonterra is
doing in terms of its Living Water programme. One of those projects has relevance in
my electorate on the Seabird Coast at Miranda and Kaiaua, where excellent work is
being done to protect the wetlands there. That is just one a rea where partnerships are
proving absolutely that they can add value to our conservation message and to our
conservation objectives.
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5365
Another one is the rat eradication on Great Mercury Island, also within the
boundaries of the very beautiful and lovely C oromandel electorate. There Sir Michael
Fay and David Richwhite have entered into a programme with the Department of
Conservation to eradicate rats on that very precious and important island. There are
some who object to that, but I think that is a wonderf ul move, and it is certainly
something that is going to enhance that island and also the greater area.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call in this
section of the estimates debate and to listen to the words of the member who just sat
down, Scott Simpson —and very fine words they were. You would believe that
everything was hunky -dory with the environment. You would not actually realise that
this is a Government that is failing in some key issues of the environment, or that we
have a Government that is not being straight with New Zealanders on a range of issues,
from the housing crisis right through to a number of issues. We certainly have a
Government that is not being straight with New Zealanders about the state of our
environment.
I just want to pick up from where Mr Simpson was concluding —he was talking
about the wonderful work in terms of our waterways. We have just received a report
from the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment that gives us the facts about
what the state of New Zealand water is, the impacts of dairying on our waterways
throughout the country, and what they are.
To stand in the House and say that everything is fine is just a symbol of how  this
Government is governing. Government members are closing their eyes to the reality and
they are closing their ears to what is happening around them. They are certainly not
being straight. In this area, our environment is being left behind.
In my address today I want to deal primarily with two key issues that we covered off
at the hearings, and my colleague Ruth Dyson will pick up on further areas. One is
Resource Management Act reform. You might remember Resource Management Act
reform. It is something  that this Government has been talking about for a very long
time. It is also something that this Government has been spending quite a lot of money
on. So when we have a look at the appropriation that this Government is putting in
under Resource Management  Act reform, we see $3 million there for contractors. One
has to assume—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: What?

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: $3 million—that is right. There is $3 million for contractors,
because this is a Government that is failing to get its reforms across the line.
It is also a Government that is failing to take the offer from Labour to work with it on
the sensible bits of Resource Management Act reform. We will —we have put that offer
in. Nicky Wagner is looking confused. She might li ke to look at the papers —it is in
there. Labour has put the offer on the table. We have said that we will work with
National on a national policy statement around housing and sensible reform —things
that can be achieved. But that has been reacted to with blankness.
There is no intention to work together for sustainable, enduring solutions for such a
linchpin piece of legislation as the Resource Management Act. Instead, we have got $3
million in this appropriation for spin doctors and contractors to play cat ch-up because
the Minister for the Environment has dropped the ball on Resource Management Act
reform. He has mucked it up from go to whoa, and not only in terms of what National
was intending to do around gutting the fundamental provisions of the Resource
Management Act. He has also mucked up relations with the coalition partners, and he
cannot get it across the line. The taxpayer is left holding the $3 million bill for Nick
Smith’s ineptitude in this particular area. The taxpayer is, of course, footing the bill for
5366 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
Nick Smith’s ineptitude in a range of areas, but in the area of Resource Management
Act reform let us just call it $3 million.
I want to turn my attention to the issue of climate change. This accounts for 48
percent of the Vote Environment budg et. It is a substantial part of the environmental
budget, and even more, actually, if you factor in the money that is set aside for the
emissions trading scheme. So after hearing speakers in the previous debate say that
Labour is the conservative, fuddy-duddy party that does not want to see progress, I have
two words for Mr Bishop—11 percent. That is the paltry sum that this Government is
thinking it is going to take to the Paris talks. It thinks that is a credible position for New
Zealand to take to the Paris talks about what our emissions reduction target should be,
but it is not.
This is a Government that is being criticised all over the world for its negligence in
this area—it is certainly not enough. This is a Government that has absolutely let the
emissions trading scheme fail to do what it needs to do, through letting the price of
carbon collapse. It is a Government that is not incentivising the things we need to be
doing around planting forests, and it is a Government that will not take the hard
decisions it needs to take around what we need to do around carbon dioxide emissions
reduction. It is a Government that will not have the sensible and needed conversation
about how we account for methane in our emissions target profile and about when we
bring this in. This is a Government that is content to be a laggard in the world and to be
criticised by other nations for not doing its bit. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Kia ora, Minister, members.
Mr Chair, ngā mihi nui ki Te Wiki o Te Reo Māori, tēnā koe.
[Thank you, Minister and members. Much accolades to Māori Language Week, and
to you, Mr Chair.]
It gives me great pleasure to stand before this Committee this afternoon and take a
call on the appropriations. From the point of view of being the Minister of
Conservation, it is very important to me that we understand the nature of the struggle
that we are involved in. It is important that we have enough money to do what we need
to do, and in order to make taxpayers’ money go even further, we need to work in
collaboration. So in my call today I am going to outline some of the more successful
collaborations, including collaboration with the Australians.
Two weeks ago I was a keynote speaker at the inaugural Threatened Species Summit
in Melbourne, where I discovered that the Australians have vastly more money than we
do to spend on many things. However, what they envy us is the level of collaboration
that we have been able to knit together with partners, philanthropists, and businesses so
that we can work as a whole team to overcome our obstacles. As New Zealand has
experienced, and so too has Australia, our vulnerable species are prone to being
predated upon by mostly eco-invaders. Ironically, here in New Zealand one of the worst
offenders for us is a treasured, protected species of possum in Australia. I did offer to
ship over a couple of million to solve both our problems, but Australia refused that kind
offer.
However, where we were able to collaborate was around the need to have a strategy
and to have what we are about to announce, which is a threatened species ambassador.
This is an individual who will help us to develop a strategy and a series of guidelines for
acting with partners, so that we will be able to do the good fight together.
I will give a couple of examples that are working successfully at the moment. One of
them is Air New Zealand. Air New Zealand is going to part -fund this threatened species
ambassador’s role for the first couple of years. That is building on a successful, l ong-
term partnership that has been worth $7 million over the past 3 years with Air New
Zealand, and it gives significant gains for conservation, our New Zealand economy, and
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5367
also Air New Zealand. It is a classic win-win, which is why it has not only sustained but
it is also being built on. Air New Zealand through its in -flight entertainment and
advertising has contributed to the success of the Department of Conservation’s Great
Walks. As we know, tourism is now our biggest earner in New Zealand. It has
overtaken dairying. By teaming up with Air New Zealand and promoting our walker
numbers, for example, those have gone up by more than 30 percent since the partnership
began. So, in round figures, that is up from 79,000 overnight stays to now more than
The Department of Conservation has also been working a lot with Genesis Energy.
That was a partnership that began 4 years ago. Over the past 5 years, $2.5 million has
been specifically aimed at supporting and protecting the blue duck, our whio, or w hio
whio as it is called in the middle part of the North Island. So what that partnership has
meant is that we have been able to double the amount of conservation work. We now
have eight secure sites to maintain a viable population of ducks that breed, and we take
out the baby ducklings —the whio whio—to actually get what we call a boot camp for
ducklings, which is where they get training in having to swim upstream on some very
rapid bits of water, so that when they are released to the wild, they are then ma de fit for
purpose in the wild. It is a fantastic thing. So welcoming partnerships with
philanthropists is also something that the Department of Conservation has encouraged
in the past couple of years.
NEXT Foundation, for example, is running $100 million  of strategic philanthropy
over the next 10 years, in partnership with the Department of Conservation and other
entities. NEXT Foundation commits something like $5 million and up to $15 million a
year, and it ring -fences three major projects including Zero  Invasive Predators, or ZIP
as it is known. Along with NEXT Foundation, Fonterra, the dairy industry, the
Department of Conservation, and the philanthropists, we are all working together. The
target is a big one. To the members of this Committee who unders tand these things, to
be able to be predator -free and to have that as a measurable target and goal by 2050 is
indeed a very ambitious target. It is only by involving philanthropists and an army of
volunteers to help us that we will be able to get there. Ze ro Invasive Predators is
focused, as we are as a Government and as a department, on excluding pests from all the
parts of the mainland where they have been eradicated.
The Department of Conservation is extremely good and effective —and is known to
be so na tionwide and internationally —at looking after pest -free islands. Our ambitious
goal now is to transfer those skills to the mainland. There are many excellent projects
that this department and this Government are involved in. I am very proud of them, and
we will continue to do our best.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe , Mr Chair. Thank you. Tuarua, ki ngā mema
o tō tātou Whare tēnā koutou katoa.
[Secondly, greetings to you all, the members of our House.]
Appointing one threatened species ambassador is not going to solve our biodiversity
crisis. The Government has done very little in this Budget to tackle that. The
Department of Conservation is not being adequately funded to tackle the conservation
challenges that it faces, and the dump of Budget documents was very revealing. It
showed that Treasury, as explained to it obviously by the Minister of Finance, does not
believe that increasing the funding for the department to assist kiwi is consistent with
the Government’s overall priorities. The Cabinet may have overruled that, but it is clear
that the Government has not got a priority of protecting our biodiversity.
Since Aotearoa New Zealand was settled 800 years ago, 53 bird species have gone
extinct, 15 of those since 1850. Currently, we rank the worst in the United Nations for
the protection of threatened species. We have more species threatened with extinction
5368 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
than any other country. Yet, what did we have in this Budget? No increase for the
Department of Conservation; in fact, there was a reduction of $7 million in the funding
that the department puts towards the management of natural heritage. This Government,
despite the Biodiversity Strategy  having a clear objective that all Government agencies
agreed to in 2000 of maintaining our biodiversity, of halting the decline, is failing to
invest adequately in the protection of our native plant species and wildlife. So the
Department of Conservation has been left to manage a third of New Zealand’s land area
and over 40,000 square kilometres of marine reserves on a pitiful budget.
Last year, for example, the department was supposed to be managing 159 threatened
species actively. What happened? The department was so distracted by the restructuring
and the loss of staff with technical expertise that it was able to actively manage only
104 threatened species. What is the target for this financial year? Managing 104
threatened species actively. The department is winding back its goals because the
Government, and thi s Minister, is not investing adequately in baseline conservation
funding. National is completely out of touch with what makes New Zealand special and
out of touch with how our wild landscapes and our native plants and wildlife contribute
to our identity as New Zealanders, and how much Kiwis value them.
We had the Department of Conservation recognised recently as the eighth most
influential brand in New Zealand, up there with Facebook and Google, and surpassed
only by TradeMe and Air New Zealand as other New Zealand entities. The 1,000
respondents in that Ipsos survey were asked to score 100 national and international
brands on five factors: leading edge, trustworthiness, engagement, citizenship, and
presence. The fact that the Department of Conservation sco red so highly shows how
much Kiwis value conservation, yet National has looked the other way when it comes to
investing in the public sector in conservation.
What it is also failing to do is use the Resource Management Act. A lot of our
threatened species  are on private land, so the decisions that Māori landowners and
private landowners make about what happens there have a major impact on whether
species like grasshoppers, like whio, and like a lot of our native fish have got better
prospects, or not, for their future. Yet we have seen this Government proposing to
spend, Nick Smith, nearly $21 million, which is allocated in this Budget for improving
resource management, for providing more advice and more tools. Yet this will not be
going to strengthen the R esource Management Act in relation to indigenous
biodiversity.
Given the National Government’s past plans to gut the Resource Management Act,
we are likely to see it further weakened and see the powers of private landholders to
make whatever decisions the y like increased. In fact, some of the past plans that the
Minister had to change the Resource Management Act have included providing for
councils to compensate private landowners if the council includes rules in the plan that
affect the ability of private  landowners to use their land. That will hinder the prospects
of threatened species. It will hinder our biodiversity, not support it.
Under National, private property rights reign supreme. We have had major evidence
of that in a recent report that Environment Canterbury has put out. It showed how
agricultural intensification is destroying areas of riparian wetland and shrubland habitat
along the margins of internationally important braided rivers in Canterbury —rivers like
the Waiau River, the Rangitata, th e Hakatere River, or the Ashburton River. Alongside
those rivers those areas of wetlands and shrublands are some of the only areas on the
Canterbury Plains where indigenous species can survive. They are habitat for kowhai,
for cabbage tree, for our native brooms, for some of the divaricating mat plants like the
Raoulia. They have not been cultivated, so they remain as habitat. Yet between 1990
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5369
and 2012 over 11,000 hectares of those areas were destroyed and converted to pasture.
That is an average of 530 hectares each year.
The Resource Management Act is supposed to provide some protection for
significant indigenous habitats and significant indigenous vegetation. It is supposed to
control the environmental effects of land use. Yet this grasp for more pasture to increase
the milk supply is leading to the decimation of remaining wild nature and indigenous
habitats on the plains. National has done absolutely nothing about that. The Department
of Conservation and Land Information New Zealand have failed to enforce the Resource
Management Act, even though 40 percent of that 11,000 hectares was actually Crown
land or conservation land or Environment Canterbury reserve. The Resource
Management Act needs strengthening to ensure that it protects our biodiversity, not
further weakening, as National is proposing in its reforms.
One of the other areas where this Government is failing our biodiversity, also under
the Resource Management Act, is the recently released National Environmental
Standard for Plantation Forestry. Although it is desirable to have some consistency in
the rules that apply to forestry across the country, we are not going to get it under this
national environmental standard. That is because it has got very weak provisions to
protect indigenous biodiversity. It has got quite clear rules around the shading of
plantations on roads to prevent icing, yet it allows exotic plantations to be established in
indigenous grasslands, and in shrublands, and it provides the requirement for resource
consent only if these areas have been identified as significant in district and regional
plans. Most councils have got a very limited list of significant natural areas. They cover
only a tiny proportion of the indigenous habitats in the district. So this National
Environmental Standard for Plantation Forestry is going to provide a mea ns for private
landowners to destroy more areas without getting a resource consent.
Again, with the biodiversity crisis, the Government could have picked up the
