National Policy Statement on Indigenous Biodiversity and made sure we had some
consistency in rules around the country in terms of vegetation clearance control. It has
failed to do that. In 2011 it could have progressed it, but it dropped it like the proverbial
hot potato because, who opposed it? Landholders and business interests. So National
has failed to implement the national policy statement under the Resource Management
Act on indigenous biodiversity. There have been two goes at that, yet this Minister and
her colleague Nick Smith have totally dropped the ball. That allows a permissive
approach to the destruction of habitat on private land to continue.
This Government is out of touch. It does not recognise that Kiwis really value our
indigenous plants and wildlife, and our wild landscapes. It does not recognise that we
need to protect these ar eas as the basis of a healthy economy. It allows private property
rights to prevail. It thinks that appointing a threatened species ambassador is going to
address the major challenges that we face with the highest number of threatened species
in the world. It fails to invest in the Department of Conservation by increasing its
funding. Instead, it cuts its funding. It is all just about optics, as my colleague Russel
Norman talked about in an earlier speech —the optics of a threatened species
ambassador, but not the substance of investing in conservation and ensuring that our
law actually protects our wild places and our indigenous habitats on private land.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : I want to speak on the Environment sector in the
Committee stage of the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill, and specifically on
climate change policy, ready for Paris 2015. This Government has a half -hearted
approach to climate change policy, and I think it has actually  lost sight of the real
objective. The need to greatly reduce the planet’s greenhouse gases arising from human
activity is the most serious issue of the age. The effects of climate change will be as
serious for New Zealand as for the rest of the world, and maybe they will be even more
5370 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
serious given New Zealand’s reliance on agriculture. New Zealand, in fact, is in a better
position than most other nations to make a positive and exemplar commitment to its
targets and, contrary to Government claims, there is no need for any risk to the New
Zealand economy by doing so. In fact, as President Clinton used to say, what is good for
the environment is good for business. Indeed, there are bound to be significant benefits
for the New Zealand economy, our physical envi ronment, our social systems, job
growth, and, of course, our international reputation from a genuine commitment to a
climate change target. Most of all, we could make the greatest contribution possible to
future generations of Kiwis by committing to a genuine and significant target for 2030.
The Government’s recently announced target of an 11 percent reduction in
greenhouse gas emissions below 1990 levels by 2030 has been called feeble,
unambitious, and embarrassing. I would have to agree. I think it is pa thetic. We in New
Zealand First do not aspire to make New Zealand First a leader in cutting greenhouse
gas emissions, but we do think there needs to be a genuine target for that and, in
particular, we think we need, as a nation, to take effective measures to ensure we
actually achieve our target. New Zealand so far has failed. Instead of doing more, this
Government has decided to take longer and to do less. There is far too much reliance on
carbon credits from plantation forests established many, many years  ago. As a result,
our actual greenhouse gas emissions will be 33 percent higher than in 1990 and we will
be worse, on a per capita basis, than the United States. Our targets are now so low that
we may not have to do anything at all to reach them, and that  applies to both the 2020
and 2030 targets. That is an utterly inadequate response, when there is no satisfactory
reason for not at least doubling the 2030 target that the Government has announced, if
not more.
The Infometrics study for the Ministry for the Environment has calculated that at
worst it would cost New Zealand as little as $500 per household—not per capita but per
household—per year, until 2020 for an additional and much more ambitious and
effective target for New Zealand. In fact, a rise to a 40 percent target instead of an 11
percent one is achievable at this reasonable and affordable cost. If you think about the
amount of $500 per household, per year, that is less than $10 per week, or, to put it
another way, it is the cost of about two cappuccinos for two people per week. It is a
very low cost indeed. That, in fact, is the real cost of an effective climate change target,
which is not what we have got under this Government. We can afford it. We can afford
a much better and much more ambitious  target, as part of our national budget. But what
we cannot afford are the risks of climate change, by doing too little.
We in New Zealand need to show the rest of the world that we are going to genuinely
play our part, not just to make a statement to the rest of the world but for our own New
Zealand benefit, especially for those of future generations. For those reasons I believe
that we must upgrade our target for Paris in December —not just to make such a
statement, but to achieve a better economy, a better social system, and a better
environment for New Zealand. I want to take this opportunity to call on the Government
to revise the target it has announced and to adopt a much more ambitious one.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: In these estimates I want
to emphasise that our National Party Government does not proclaim to be the greenest
party in this Parliament. What we do proclaim is that we are the party  that is able to
marry together good economic stewardship with responsible management of New
Zealand’s treasured environment.
I firstly want to respond to the challenge from Eugenie Sage around biodiversity. My
colleague Maggie Barry, the new Minister of Conservation—against the advice of
Treasury—secured $11.5 million in this vote for ensuring that the ongoing decline in
the kiwi population does not continue, and if there is a portion of our biodiversity that
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5371
every member of this Committee should treasure , it is the survival of our iconic kiwi
bird.
I want to respond to the contribution by New Zealand First in respect of New
Zealand’s climate change target and the work that Tim Groser is doing internationally. I
want to put on the record of the House, as a member who has taken an interest in
climate change for all of my 25 years here, that I have not known a climate change
Minister to be as influential in the international negotiations as Tim Groser, and every
member of this Parliament should be proud of t he contribution that he is making. Mr
Denis O’Rourke challenges us on the target of a 30 percent reduction of emissions by
2030. I have a simple challenge for New Zealand First: we could have been much more
ambitious in those targets if it were not for the fact that emissions went up by 25 percent
in the term of the previous Labour Government, which New Zealand First was part of.
So it is rich for New Zealand First to come to this Parliament and claim that the target is
not ambitious enough when, during its  watch, when its members were in the Cabinet
room, emissions went up by more than in any other term.
Look back at the projection—the actual record of emissions between 1990, when we
entered the framework convention on climate change, and today —and the ver y worst
period was in the period from 2005 to 2008. At the same time that the previous Labour
Government was talking about carbon neutrality —the very period when New Zealand
First had ministerial warrants —New Zealand’s emissions went through the roof. I as k
those members to contrast the fact that the actual record of this Government in
constraining the growth of emissions has been more successful than any Government in
the records since 1990.
What these estimates provide for is a real focus on the environm ental issues that are
important to New Zealand. The biggest increase in my vote is in terms of the work
around fresh water. I think every member of this Committee would want that to be a
priority for the Government. Let me give the numbers, for a matter of  record. These
estimates enable us to lift the overall contribution during our period in Government —
our commitment to freshwater clean -up projects—to $350 million over the 9 years that
we have been in Government. Let me compare that with times when there w as a lot
more cash for the Government, when the previous Labour Government spent just $50
million. That is one -seventh of the amount that we have committed, and that is why I
say to members of this Committee that this Government has a record of real
commitments in fresh water.
But it is not enough just to commit the money; we need to get the proper rules and
management in place to manage fresh water. That is why, in 2010, we introduced the
first National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management and why, in 2013, we
introduced national standards, known as the National Objectives Framework, and why,
in this next year, we will be taking the next steps around the invertebrates index, around
the issues of exceptions to the policy, and around the very tricky, c hallenging issue
around Māori rights and interests. With these estimates we will be able to take those
next key steps around fresh water.
I also want to say that these estimates provide the resources for the Government to
take the next steps in ocean mana gement. An important step that we will be taking later
this year is for the Environmental Protection Authority to take responsibility for the
pollution regulations in that part of the exclusive economic zone that makes up more
than 20 percent of the area t hat we are responsible for in terms of jurisdiction. That is
why a very important part of our next steps for our Bluegreen team is around reform of
New Zealand’s legislation in respect of marine-protected areas.
This is a complex piece of work. It involves a large number of Government
agencies—foreign affairs and defence have an interest, and both my ministry, the
5372 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
Ministry for the Environment, and the Department of Conservation. There is a big
interest, of course, from the Ministry for Primary Industries, and Nathan Guy is taking
an intense interest in it. This year we will be putting out a substantive discussion
document on how we can improve the legislative framework, and that is something we
are going to do in t he next year and we would welcome Labour’s support for a piece of
work that has been promised for—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Got a time frame yet?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I will just remind the Labour member that it was in
Labour’s policy in 1999. You had 9 years in Government and made no progress. Look
forward to the progress that we will be making in the next year around that important
piece of work around marine -protected areas, which was mentioned in the Speech from
the Throne at the beginning of this year.
The other specific area that I want to mention is the importance of resource
management reform. In that area we are going in the direction of a greater degree of
national consistency. If we are to get good environmental outcomes but bring the
compliance costs down for sectors, what we need to have is a greater use of the national
instruments under the Resource Management Act. That is why right now, with the
support of these estimates, which provide a substantive increase in funding, we are
looking at a national environment standard on telecommunications. Why? Because my
colleague Amy Adams, the Minister for Communications, is going for broke to make
sure that New Zealand is a world leader in the extension of ultra -fast broadband and
cellphone technologies.
But it is no good doing that if we cannot actually get those new networks consented.
Having every single one of our councils across New Zealand having a different set of
rules around where you can put Wi -Fi, ultra-fast broadband, and cellphones does not
make sense. That is why these estimates provide for our concluding this year a national
environment standard around those communications. I really do challenge the Green
Party, which has come out publicly and opposed that national environment standard,
and I say that it is holding back New Zealand’s connectedness and New Zealand’s
competitive advantage in not wanting us to have a greater degree of consistency in that
area.
I will also mention one of New Zealand’s really important e xport industries, the
forestry sector. You know, members give lip- service to the issue of regional
development. What are the regions of New Zealand where forestry is a critical industry?
It is Northland. It is the central North Island. It is areas like Nel son, Marlborough, and
Southland. If you talk to the forestry industry, one of the real concerns that that sector
has is differentiation of rules under the Resource Management Act, which drives up
their costs and undermines their international competitivene ss. That new national
environment standard, which we are consulting on right now, is going to provide for
good environmental outcomes. In some areas it will mean tougher environmental
rules—that is true —but it will result in better environmental outcomes a nd a huge
reduction in the amount of bureaucracy and consents that are required for New
Zealand’s fourth-biggest export earner.
Alongside that piece of work is important work around the Resource Management
Act, which is also critical in respect of the key  challenge New Zealand has around
housing. A key part of these estimates provides support for the development of the
Auckland Unitary Plan. Why does that matter? Well, Auckland is actually one -third of
the country. This Government is providing support to A uckland to be able to finalise a
plan for that city in the next year, which is so critical to its economic growth and
housing, as well as ensuring that we have good environmental management in that year.
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5373
So this programme in the conservation, climate chan ge, and environmental areas
shows a very active blue -green agenda by this Government. It does the things that will
make sure we better manage our environment, our water, our marine space, our
biodiversity, our air quality—those things—while also supporting a strong economy.
Undermining all that work, then, is a revolutionary step in the way in which we
actually measure how we are doing.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Did you say “undermining” or “underlining”?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Underlining—absolutely underlining it. Let me tell the
member who has interjected why. It is this: if you ask me what is one of the two most
important pieces of legislation that a National Government has passed that has made
New Zealand do better, I would highlight the Fiscal Responsibility Act 1994, because
we, as a country, should be ashamed of our record preceding that Act in the
management of our public finances. And in the 20 years hence we have done so much
better.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Rau rakatira mā, tēnei te mihi ki a
koutou i runga i te kaupapa o te rā, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
[To the esteemed ones of a hundredfold, I acknowledge you collectiv ely in regard to
the matter of the day; salutations, greetings, and accolades to you and to us all.]
It is a really important debate that we are having and I want to acknowledge
everyone who has contributed to it. It is the one opportunity in the year tha t select
committees get a chance to hold the Ministers of various portfolios to account, and I
want to acknowledge the Ministers who did front up to the committees and generally
answered questions to the best of their ability—not always as well as we had h oped, but
certainly to the best of their ability.
There are few comments that I want to make in relation to the conservation portfolio
specifically. This is the seventh year in a row that we have seen a reduction in the
overall budget for the Department of Conservation, and, frankly, it is getting to the point
where every time the department has a bit of crisis on its hands—for example, a stoat on
Kāpiti—it puts out the begging bowl and has to ask whether there is anybody who
would like to donate so that i t can perform its core statutory responsibilities. I think that
that is an embarrassment to New Zealand and New Zealanders, and I think the Ministers
misrepresent the position that the department has been put in by the lack of support
from their Cabinet colleagues.
There are other points of concern that were raised during the debate in the Local
Government and Environment Committee that I want to mention. The first is the lack of
reclassification of stewardship land and the implication that that might have ,
particularly in two areas that are of current concern. One is Ruataniwha and the other is
the Hurunui, where conservation land is being proposed as part of a land swap for the
creation of a dam. Because those areas, in the most part, are currently stewar dship land,
there has been a tendency to reduce the public concern by dismissing them as land of
little value, and we know from the work that the Parliamentary Commissioner for the
Environment has done on the need for the proper classification of stewardship land that
that land is often not of low value at all. I would really urge the Minister for the
Environment and the Minister of Conservation to take the report of the Parliamentary
Commissioner for the Environment and do something with it.
The second co ncern that I want to put on the record is the fact that the Minister for
the Environment is now responsible for leading our marine reserves legislation and
change, and I want to say that that is not because of the personality of the Minister for
the Environment. Few National members are more passionate than he is about marine
protection, and I acknowledge the work that he has done over recent years in particular.
5374 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
That is not the concern that I have. The concern I have is that as Minister for the
Environment, he operates under different criteria.
The current marine protection legislation led by the Minister of Conservation has
preservation and protection as the basis of that legislation, whereas the exclusive
economic zone legislation, which is where the Minister for the Environment is likely to
lead, has a sustainable management ethos. They are quite different foundations and that
causes a considerable concern in the transfer. So it is not about the personality of the
Hon Dr Nick Smith. I am quite comfortabl e with him, amongst all of the National
Government Ministers —in fact, he is the only one amongst all of the National
Government Ministers who, I think, gives a toss in this area. It is about what the basis of
our future marine legislation is going to be. So I wish him every success in ensuring that
conservation and preservation are the basis of future legislation.
The next point I want to mention is the inability of the Minister of Conservation to
answer, on time, some of the questions and her refusal to a nswer questions about
unsuccessful Budget bids. She is the only Minister I have seen before a select
committee who has refused to acknowledge that in some areas her bids were
unsuccessful. She should have been up front and honest with not just the committe e and
Parliament but the public of New Zealand. I have seen other Ministers front up to those
questions; she refused. I have subsequently asked the Prime Minister; he has refused to
have anything to do with that as well.
The last point I want to make is in regard to conservation partnerships. Of course
these are a good thing —working with philanthropic organisations, with business, with
individuals, and with community organisations together to progress a shared goal —but
it goes over the line of partnership when the department is dependent on donations in
order to fulfil its core functions. It has got that way in the area of pest management and
control, it has got that way in areas of planting, and it has got that way in the area of
education. Those are core statutory functions that the department is unable to perform
on its own.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: E Te Whare tēnā koe; tuarua, ki ngā mema o tō tātou
Whare, tēnā koutou katoa; tuatoru, mihi atu ki Te Wi ki o Te Reo Māori, tēnā koutou,
tēnā tātou katoa.
[I greet you the House; secondly, salutations to you all, the members of our House;
and, thirdly, I acknowledge Māori Language Week. Greetings to you and to us all.]
I am addressing my comments to the Vote Environment budget. The revenue line
shows that the waste disposal levy is expected to remain the same for the 2015- 16 year
as it did for the 2014-15 year. Currently, that budget is $32 million.
This revenue is the result of charging $10 on every tonne of waste that goes to
landfill, and I would just note that that is in the Waste Minimisation Act 2008, which
was a member’s bill initiated by the Green Party that got cross -party support. That levy
of $32 million is shared between local government and central government to fund
waste minimisation activities and initiatives. Basically, that is what it is used for.
The Government’s Budget line shows that waste minimisation is not working —
certainly not if it is going to keep the revenue level at the same amount as this year and
last year —and I guess that is not really a surprise when you consider some of the
schemes t hat the Government is funding. The classic example is the one that the
Minister announced on the Saturday before last, which was a voluntary product
stewardship scheme from the packaging industry, where it would set up collection
points at supermarkets as a 3 -year trial to collect single -use plastics and soft plastics,
including single-use plastic bags.
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5375
The Government has allocated $1.2 million to do this for the 3- year trial, but it is an
example of “greenwashing”, and nobody is fooled. One just has to look at the New
Zealand Herald editorial on Saturday, which basically explained why it is
“greenwashing”. Again, today in the Dominion Post we have the headline here, “Plastic
bag scheme won’t work”, over an opinion piece from Massey University’s Dr Trisia
Farrelly. It will not work because the scheme is an ambulance at the bottom of the cliff,
and it does not deal with the problem of single -use plastic bags in the environment. We
use 1.6 billion of these single -use plastic bags every year. That generates abo ut 6 to 11
tonnes of carbon per year, and if we got rid of them, it would be the same as taking
about 3,600 cars off the road permanently.
Plastic bags are designed to be disposed of. Yes, they do not make up a huge amount
in the landfill, but that is bec ause they are incredibly lightweight, and this is where they
have a devastating impact on the environment. They can be ingested by marine
animals—up to 2,000 different marine species, including whales and turtles, are known
to ingest plastic bags and die f rom them —and they break down into micro- plastic,
which is eaten by fish and then it enters the human food chain.
This Government scheme does not work to change consumer behaviour, so it does
not minimise the amount of soft, single -use plastic, and it targ ets the same
environmentally aware consumers who already take their reusable shopping bags to the
supermarket in the first place. This is the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff, once we
have failed to avoid, refuse, and reduce, and then we have got into recycling, but this is
not going to fix it.
Prevention is the way to go, and for single -use plastic bags, that would be done by
introducing a disincentive to use them. We could join hundreds of countries and States
across the world and phase them out entirely, or we could introduce a point-of-sale levy.
International evidence shows that having a levy reduces single -use plastic bag use by
between 70 percent and 95 percent, depending on how much is charged. Local
government bodies really, really support doin g this. They voted on the Sunday before
last to call on the Government to introduce a levy on single -use plastics because they
are the ones that are cleaning up the waterways and cleaning up the drains that are
getting blocked by this pest and this terrible product, which is having a huge impact on
our environment.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: E Te Heamana e mihi atu ana ki a
koe.
[I acknowledge you, Mr Chairman.]
I would like to spend just a few moments talking about the conservation partnerships,
but if I can just acknowledge the Minister in the chair, Nick Smith. He spoke to the key
messages that he actually spoke to at the select committee. He spoke about our reform
agenda over the last few years and how effective that has been. We have the National
Policy Statement for Freshwater, the National Objectives Framework, the
Environmental Protection Authority —there is a huge list of reforms and, of course,
there are funding initia tives to support that. But, in particular, I would like to spend a
few moments just reflecting on the conservation partnerships that we now have in place,
have had in place for a number of years, and intend to continue to invest heavily in over
the next 2 or 3 years.
When these conservation partnerships were introduced a few years ago under Nick
Smith, and under Al Morrison’s leadership as the chief executive, there was a typical
reaction from the Labour Party and the Green Party in particular. They were very anti
them—a typically ideological reaction from those who think that conservation and
business cannot work together and are in fact, in their view, very incompatible
5376 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
bedfellows. But these partnerships have proven that wrong. The philosophy that we
were privatising the Department of Conservation, that private -public partnerships are
evil, and that conservation is simply the preserve of the Government reflects a tired and
captured ideology that, in my view, is holding them back.
These conservation partnerships, which Minister Barry and Lou Sanson stepped us
through in the Local Government and Environment Committee, are successful and are
working. The reason they are successful and working is that they are partnering with
people who are on the ground. They have the expertise of the Department of
Conservation, which is in the particular region, understands the ecosystem pressures,
and can identify what the appropriate interventions are to give the best outcome. You
have local communities, be they iwi or be they local non- government partnerships, that
are energised and are passionate for their particular area, and they can be partnered with
business in a way that delivers real benefit. It is not a failed ideology of privatisation,
which gets barked at us from the other side. It is, yet again, an example of a pragmatic
framework that is working and is delivering, and I am very pleased to able to be part of
a Government that supports that and to hear from Minister Barry in terms of the various
partnerships and how they are progressing.
Some of this is pretty personal to me because of the Fonterra Living Waters
programme, which was launched 2 years ago in partnership with the Department of
Conservation. I was part of that; I saw it being introduced. Five areas across the count ry
that are under pressure are having an immediate turn -round, with the community,
Fonterra, and the Department of Conservation working together to get a better
ecosystem outcome. It is the same with Air New Zealand. There is a list of them, and it
is worth just reflecting on these conservation partnerships and how they are impacting
across the country, from Air New Zealand’s conservation partnership —which was
initially focused on supporting the kiwi and has now been broadened to supporting
Great Walks, mar ine reserves, and other coastal gems —to Dulux New Zealand.
Obviously, I have touched on Fonterra’s partnership. There is Genesis Energy and its
support in terms of the Whio Forever Project. Minister Barry, of course, at the select
committee spoke on the Ki wis for Kiwi programme and the significant investment that
we are putting in for that programme, and the Mitre 10 Takahē Rescue programme is
also an example of that.
What is coming to be very clear to those who are involved in these partnerships is
that o nce you actually get around the table likeminded people —people who are
concerned about ensuring a better ecosystem outcome —and businesses that are
prepared to put their money and support and energy behind that, over time, as they work
together on that part icular programme, other opportunities come from that. As the
relationships become deeper and as the community, the Department of Conservation,
and the business have an established track record of being able to work together for
effect, the community is presented with more opportunities to take up.
I want to reinforce that that is an example of a public policy that is working. It is
working today, and it deserves ongoing support and credit, not the blind opposition
based on ideology that we are hearing from the other side.
Earlier on we had Eugenie Sage talking about the fact there was no new money in
this Budget for conservation. That is wrong. There is $11.2 million of extra funding.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Kaiwhakahaere. Ā, koutou rā, te Pāti
Rōpū Reipa, Ngā Kākāriki, Aotearoa Tuatahi, me ngā Kahurangi he mihi tēnei ki a
koutou katoa.
[Thank you, Mr Chair. To you, the Labour Party, the Greens, New Zealand First,
and the Blues, I acknowledge you all.]
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5377
I would like to take a short call in the estimates debate around the environment
sector. From listening to the different views from both sides of the House, indeed the
glass on this side of the House is half full, or over half full, and on the  other side,
unfortunately, it is empty, or half empty.
I just want to also acknowledge the last speaker, my colleague Todd Muller, who
talked particularly about the relationships that have been developed and fostered,
particularly over the last three term s of this Government. I particularly want to
acknowledge Lou Sanson as well, because when we look at the work that he has done,
particularly with iwi, mana whenua, and tangata whenua, there has not been a time ever
during the history of the Department of C onservation when iwi relationships have been
so high. That is a true reflection of the way that the Department of Conservation
acknowledges Te Ao Māori, the world of the Māori, and particularly because the other
part of it is a whakataukī, or an interesting proverb, that goes “Whatungarongaro he
tangata, toitū he whenua”. What that means is that people move on, but the land
remains. That is really the basis around true partnership and relationships when we talk
about the environment.
There is one part of t he estimates vote that I would just like concentrate on, and it
particularly concerns the Minister of Conservation, but that is not to forget the other two
Ministers, Minister Groser, particularly with climate change, and Minister Smith as
well, for the en vironment. The Minister of Conservation appeared before the Local
Government and Environment Committee to update us around the programmes to tackle
kauri die-back. I want to just really concentrate on this, because some years ago I spent
some time working in tourism up in Northland —particularly up in Waipoua working
with the iwi of Te Uri o Hau, which is an iwi that operates right inside the Waipoua
Forest—and also working with Footprints Waipoua, which does tours, particularly to
Tāne Māhuta, and really tells this incredible story around the spirituality of Waipoua.
While I was there I really did gain an appreciation for how much of a taoka, or
treasure, kauri are to tangata whenua of the Tai Tokerau but also to all New Zealanders.
In the area sometimes referred to as the Kauri Coast, kauri contributes to a growing
tourist industry as well. I had the opportunity when I was up there in Northland at the
beginning of the year to visit the Kauri Museum at Matakohe. That also demonstrated
the really important part that kauri plays in the local economy.
I just want to say that it is fascinating when you look at those people who work on
this kauri die -back programme, because it really reflects the partnership that the
Department of Conservation has developed with them. You do have these individuals,
you have conservationists, you have iwi, and then you have the Department of
Conservation working together. So when we look at this —when the Minister came to
the committee she expressed the frustration that I think we a ll feel that we do not know
enough about the invisible killer of the kauri. What we do know is that the pathogen is
carried through the soil, and that it is easily spread from place to place on our shoes and
by visitors.
A party vote  was called for on the  question, That Vote Conservation, Vote
Environment, and Vote Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment be agreed to.
Ayes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 58
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 12.
Votes agreed to.
5378 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
External Sector

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, we now come to the votes for
the external sector —volume B.5, volume 4. The question is that Vote Customs, Vote
Defence, Vote Defence Force, Vote Foreign Affairs and Trade, and Vote Official
Development Assistance stand part of the schedules. I ask the chair of the committee to
set out the major findings of your committee in relation to the estimates.
MARK MITCHELL (Chairperson of the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade
Committee): I have a lot to say in such a short time, but I will give it my best sho t. I
wanted to speak about Vote Foreign Affairs first and then cover off very quickly what
we discussed in our appropriation hearing in the committee. The first thing is, of course,
the sheep farm in Saudi Arabia. I just want to say that from my own observations from
my own time up in the Middle East, I was very interested to watch a big stock -handling
facility that was built in Boosaaso. It was sponsored by the Qatari Government. It was
built so that the state of Puntland, which is a part of Somalia on the  Horn of Africa,
could start trading livestock with Saudi Arabia because of the size of the market and the
demand there. It helped drive up its GDP. It was a very good project.
I also want to state that mutton and lamb is a big part of the diet in the Mid dle East.
That is not something new. It is not like we are just taking sheep into the Middle East
for the first time —they are there. The markets in Basra in southern Iraq used to feed a
good part of the Middle East prior to the second war, and people would travel from all
over the Middle East to go to the markets and the stockyards in Basra to buy mutton.
We were told that no additional funds had been provided to New Zealand Trade and
Enterprise to actually fund the agribusiness hub there, and there are about 30 New
Zealand businesses connected to the agribusiness hub that are providing goods and
services. This is a big business. This has a lot of potential for New Zealand. We own a
lot of the intellectual property, the knowledge, and the know how in order to actually
create a real, vibrant business in the Middle East.
We spoke about the Trans-Pacific Partnership agreement. We asked for an update on
that. The agreement is an important one for New Zealand. It involves 40 percent of New
Zealand’s trade in goods and services and it involves five of New Zealand’s top 10
trading partners. We know that once the agreement is signed by all parties, it will go
through New Zealand’s domestic approval processes, in the course of which the
agreement and its associated n ational interest analysis will come before the Foreign
Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee. If changes are required to New Zealand’s
domestic legislation, Parliament will need to pass them before ratification of the treaty.
We spoke about the ASEAN relat ionship. The year 2015 is the 40 th anniversary of
New Zealand’s diplomatic relations with ASEAN countries, and New Zealand will host
31 celebratory events across 10 ASEAN capitals.
We talked about Niue. The Minister of Foreign Affairs spoke about Niue. He
highlighted that since 2010 New Zealand has focused its support to Niue on the
development of its tourism industry, at the request of the country’s Premier and
Government. We heard that Niue’s visitor numbers have increased considerably and
that this has been a very, very successful initiative, which has been supported by New
Zealand.
We asked the Minister about our seat on the United Nations Security Council, of
which I am personally very proud to see him now sitting in the president’s seat. I want
to acknowledge him, all of our ambassadors —for example, Sir Jim McLay, whom we
spoke to on the weekend —and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade for being so
successful in securing us a seat on the Security Council.
We have begun our month-long presidency. In that time we are going to host an open
debate in the council on 30 July, in which countries from outside the council can
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5379
participate. This is important. This is significant because this is one of the points that we
lobbied on in trying to gain support to actually win that seat on the Security Council.
They are going to be talking about the security challenges facing developing small
Island States. Although such States make up about one quarter of the membership of the
United Nations, only three of them have ever served on the Security Council. New
Zealand wants to provide an opportunity for the wider group to be heard on the council.
We also plan to have an informal, closed dialogue on reform of the Security Council to
make it more accountable and more t ransparent, and there is going to be a fair bit of
focus around the use of the veto.
The Minister spoke briefly about the Middle East peace process. He highlighted the
fact that having a seat on the United Nations Security Council will affect our
involvement in the Middle East peace process, and that there is general consensus that
after the Israeli elections and the formation of its Government, the Security Council
talks on Iran also need to be concluded before the Middle East peace process can be
addressed. There may be an opportunity in August or September to consider the peace
process, and New Zealand will be alert to playing an active role in the process, on which
the international community agrees urgent action is needed. So you can see that t he
Minister and the ministry are going to be very active on the Security Council.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: I want to speak to the New Zealand
Defence Force estimates and to begin by saying that at the estimates hearing, having the
Minister of Defence before the committee is a real test of whether the Minister has any
knowledge or understanding of his portfolio. I regret to report to the Committee that 8
months into his portfolio Gerry Brownlee does not understand defence. He has not got a
clue about it.
It was interesting. We started with a fairly light issue. “Light issue” is a play on
words, I guess, because it was about obesity problems in the Defence Force. That week
there had been a major article in the paper saying that 20 percent of the Defence Force
personnel were obese and 10 percent were significantly obese, and the Minister said that
he did not know anything about it. To give credit to Mark Mitchell, he said: “But surely,
Minister, if you banned fizzy drinks and deep- fried food from the armed services’
canteen, there must be a problem?”. And Gerry Brownlee said: “Oh, we were just
following what Labour did in the schools 4 years earlier.” I want to know how come it
is that “ nanny State Gerry Brownlee” will stop adults in employment from drinking
fizzy drinks but the Government removed the requirement not to put those things on the
shelves of school cafes, in order to look after the kids. That was curious.
Then there was a question about Vanuatu. Vanuatu—we were a bit late getting there.
We have a great ship, the Canterbury , to do the job in Vanuatu, and the Minister said:
“Well, we can’t send our people up there till we know what they want.” We know what
they want from day on e. When there is a cyclone, they need building materials, they
need water purifiers, they need food, and they need equipment to move the debris. But
we took 2 weeks to get there and we did not put the NH90s in there, as the Australians
did. What did Gerry Brownlee say? I have got it here. He said the NH90s were “a
dreadful purchase”. Well, I want to read to the Committee the answers to two questions
that I asked the Minister in the written questions for estimates: “Does the Minister stand
by the assessment of the NH90 aircraft by his predecessors the Hon Wayne Mapp and
the Hon Jonathan Coleman as being ‘very capable’ and ‘a quantum leap forward for
New Zealand’?”. The response from Gerry Brownlee was “Yes”— yes! He said it was
“a dreadful purchase” but it was a quantum leap forward, according to his predecessors,
and he agreed.
Then I asked “Has the RNZAF ever advised the Minister that the NH90s are not and
will not be fit for purpose?”, and the answer was no. I want to tell the Minister how
5380 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
angry the people are in the Royal New Zealand Air Force about his disparaging of the
best rotary wing aircraft they have ever had.
But the real questions came on the deployment to Iraq. I sat down and read the New
York Times when I was at an international airport, about t he same time as the inquiry
was going on. What did the New York Times  report? It reported that the United States
military in Iraq had more than three times the capacity for training Iraqi soldiers than
was being used. They had 2,000 soldiers being trained. They had capacity for 6,700. So

items.speaker: I have got to ask the question
items.text: why are we spending $65 million and putting our capable
troops at risk to have 16 trainers go to Iraq when there is already a surplus of trainers in
that country? The article went on to say t hat the other problem is that there are 22,000
Iraqi troops who have deserted and 50,000 ghost soldiers, where the money is being
ripped off and put into the private pockets of those running the military leadership.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I rise to take a call in respect of the trade
estimates. There are two issues that I want to address. The first issue is in respect of the
sheep saga, which was traversed a little at the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade
Committee, and as members who were there will know, the National Government
members did their best to stop us inquiring into that. They gave the Minister, the Hon
Murray McCully, the opportunity to explain things from his perspective and to try to
cover his tracks, and then they stopped us from inquiring into it properly. This is part of
the orchestrated cover up that we have had from the Government in respect of the Saudi
sheep saga. Even now, we and just about every media organisation in New Zealand
have outstanding Official Information Act requests that have been routinely ignored, in
breach of the Act, by all of the ministries —by New Zealand Trade and Enterprise, by
the Ministry of Foreign Affairs  and Trade, by the Ministry for Primary Industries, by
the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, and by Treasury. They have all
gone to the end of the statutory period and have then all claimed that they need more
time. Then Treasury had the audacity to say that it was going to have a proactive release
some time in the distant future.
At the heart of this is the fact that the Government has been caught acting
unscrupulously. It has wasted more than $6 million on a farm in the desert, where most
of the lambs died. The Minister for Primary Industries, Nathan Guy, said he thought that
it might have been because of a sand storm, which is rather ironic given that the farm
advisers say it was more likely to have been a rain event, which is, itself, ironic given
that the sheep are under shelter. That waste of $6 million is less unprincipled than the $4
million facilitation payment that the Government paid unnecessarily in order to settle
what it says was some threatened legal claim, which we now know was never
threatened. There has never been any legal advice that we have been able to see that
says there was any legal risk to be settled. It was a facilitation payment paid to the Al-
Khalaf Group—a $4 million upfront payment that was hidden for a number of years and
that has still not been properly explained by Mr McCully.
As if that was not bad enough, we have also had the South Korea free -trade
agreement, which makes some important advances in terms of tariff reductions for New
Zealand, and, therefore, is g ood for our traders. But, again, we had to drag out from the
Government and from officials the truth that the South Korea free -trade agreement
contains a limitation on a future New Zealand Government extending the sorts of
categories of investment that are  screened for —i.e., you can screen for existing
categories of investment like farms but you cannot add a new category of screening like
banning the purchase of houses. It is almost unbelievable that the Government could be
so inept as to get this wrong in respect of the South Korea free-trade agreement, because
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5381
the recent South Korea free -trade agreement with Australia permits just that: the
banning of the sale of houses to South Koreans. So why this Government was so
negligent as to trade the sovereignty o f a future Government being able to do that I do
not know.
As if that was not bad enough, we have then had denial after denial in this House,
where the Minister of Trade has refused to answer questions as to whether the same
mistake is being made in the Tr ans-Pacific Partnership. They have insulted the
intelligence of this House by refusing to answer questions when exactly the same
questions were answered by Minister Groser on The Nation and on Q+A  at the
weekend, and then by the Prime Minister on Q+A  on Sunday. It is a disgraceful thing.
Lots of my forebears came to New Zealand to escape absentee landlords, and yet that is
what this Government is allowing to happen in New Zealand. The richest 1 percent in
the world from overseas countries who want to put their money beyond the reach of
their authorities or to spread their investments, or who think that New Zealand is a safe
place to put their money, can outbid New Zealanders, can push up house prices, and can
exclude New Zealanders from owning one house in their own country.
We have seen a documentary in Australia of the problems that it is having in respect
of farmland purchases at the moment; another area where this Government allows
overly permissive rules. This Government pretended after the Shanghai Pengxin
transaction that it was tightening the rules, and then it sent a side letter to the Overseas
Investment Office telling it to look felicitously or to approve applications for up to 10
times the size of the average farm unit.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: E te Tiamana, tēnā koe. As
Minister of Customs Te Mana Arai o Aotearoa it is my pleasure to update the House on
the excellent work of the New Zealand Customs Service and our Budget initiatives. It is
an enormous privilege to be the Minister of Customs because it is the oldest New
Zealand service. It is celebrating its 175 th anniversary this year, because the first
customs house was established in Russell weeks before the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840.
I like to say that customs is 175 years young, because even though it is a traditional
organisation and it has loyalty and commi tment, it is innovative and forward- thinking
and it delivers cutting -edge services and technology. So it is great to see that you can
teach an old dog new tricks.
Customs has four major roles. The first is protecting the border, the second is
managing travellers as they cross that border, the third is managing imports and exports,
and the fourth is collecting revenue. Over that 175 years the demands at the borders
have changed, but they are always challenging, because customs’ job is to keep New
Zealand an d New Zealanders safe. We do that by managing risk and making border
access as quick, as easy, and as cost -effective as possible for legitimate travellers and
goods, but as complicated, as difficult, as time -consuming, and as expensive as possible
for illegal or dangerous people or goods. The New Zealand Customs Service does this
very well. The World Economic Forum rates New Zealand as fourth in the world for
facilitating trade across the border and sixth in the world for its actual border
processing. That is pretty amazing considering the emphasis we have on biosecurity and
the fact that other countries do not do that at all.
Last year 10.4 million travellers crossed our border, and those numbers are
increasing every year. They are increasing in number and  in diversity. We have more
non-English speaking travellers and we have different cultures, and that increases the
complexity at the border. SmartGate allows us to manage that risk. Just this week I
announced 29 new SmartGates. These are SmartGates on ster oids. These are
SmartGates that are brand new technology with a one- step process. No more ticketing
5382 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
booths. No more two queues. It has faster processing and better-quality biometrics. That
is a fantastic upgrade for New Zealand.
We are also delivering for  importers and exporters of goods. The Joint Border
Management System and the Trade Single Window are world -leading technologies.
They are transforming border processes and streamlining systems. Recently I visited the
US, and talking to customs officials a nd business people there they were absolutely
impressed that New Zealand had this technology —and jealous, because they do not
have it yet. Customs manages about 11 million import and export transactions, and 99
percent of those are managed within 30 minute s. We are also actively supporting
exporters. Whenever the Government negotiates any trade agreements, customs is
involved in order to manage the border processes. In Budget 2015, $6.2 million has
been allocated over 4 years to support small businesses so that they can access
international markets and reduce the risk of trade disruption.
We are constantly challenged at the border by people who want to bring illegal or
dangerous things into New Zealand by smuggling drugs, offensive weapons, and child
pornography. So we need to be vigilant and we need to be one step ahead, and we do
that by working in partnership with the New Zealand Police and with international
agencies. In the last 6 months we have stopped half a tonne of methamphetamine at our
border. That is a street value of $246 million. We know that we are holding our own
against the drug rings and organised crime because the price of methamphetamine has
remained the same since 2011, so we have control.
We also collect revenue for the Crown. We collect about $12 billion every year.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Te mihi nui ki Te
Wiki o Te Reo, Te Reo rangatira, Te Reo tino ātaahua, Te Reo tūturu, Te Reo kotahi o
Aotearoa.
[I salute Māori Language Week, the noble language, the beautiful language, the
original language, and the sole language of New Zealand.]
Before I speak about overseas assistance and aid I would like to talk just a little bit
about foreign affairs as that is part of the appropriation. How is the war going? How is
that going—$65 million worth of it? How is the Trans -Pacific Partnership agreement
going—that thing that was never going to take away our medicines but we have found
out, just today, that it is going to take away our cheap medicines? It is going really well,
if you do not think about the real value of the way we use our money in this country.
The way we make trade deals, the way we actually approach peace and defence is a bit
of a disaster, and so foreign affairs at the moment, defence —a number of these
portfolios that are covered by this appropriation—are actually a real mess.
We have actually done really well in helping to polarise things further in the Middle
East and at the same time, in  another appropriation, we are refusing to take any more
refugees except the bare minimum. So on the one hand $65 million is going to promote
the wars that create more polarisation; on the other hand we are not going to help people
whose lives are destroyed by war. So that is a really great start for foreign affairs.
I would like to talk, however, about overseas development and assistance because it
is our privilege to be in Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa, the Pacific, the wonderful Pacific, where
we have relationshi ps with a number of Pacific nations. Some of those relationships
ought to include a healthy and honest relationship around aid, because we are the
privileged, the wealthy, and the exploiter, in some cases, of the cheap labour of the
Pacific—we have been in  the past —and so we need to have a robust and ethical
overseas development and assistance aid programme.
Under the current Government it has become very economics -focused and to our
shame there is no more of it. In fact, in 2014 our appropriation was 0.27 percent of
gross national income (GNI) compared with 0.39 percent for most OECD members. So
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5383
other countries of a similar size are doing a whole lot better but, unfortunately, the
Government is a bit mean, a little bit selfish, and is not prepared to go for the real goal
for official development assistance, which would be 0.7 percent of GNI. We can be the
better country because we rely on the relationships we have in the Pacific. Just because
we are bigger and more powerful does not mean we should change ou r aid policies or
freeze our aid policies to what they were way back in the old days. If the defence budget
can be increased why cannot the official development assistance budget be increased?
We are going to make more peace in this world through those aid and development
healthy relationships than we are ever going to make by sending people over to kill
people who already think that killing people is the solution.
So I think it is quite important to look closely at official development assistance and
look at what it should be addressing. We are on the Security Council. We are in a
position to talk about security and aid, and all of those things should be focused on
addressing climate change, engendering more local participation and gender equity —
dare I say it, as if anyone saw the New Zealand Herald story today they will know that
the Government is not really not very big on gender equity at the moment; its statistics
are shameful—but particularly overseas, looking at the economic and social rights of
recipient countries.
So official development assistance needs to be strengthened and it needs to be
increased, and there needs to be support for the right kind of development. I said this in
this Parliament—was it 2 years ago; I cannot quite recall, maybe less —when we had a
wonderful conference here, which the Government did host and fund, for Pacific nations
to come and talk about the important issues of the Pacific. It was a great conference.
The greatest thing about it was its rejection of the Government ’s free-trade agenda and
the Pacific nations’ rejection of opening their economies—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: I don’t remember that.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Mr —I cannot remember his title —the Hon Mr
Bridges forgets that in the last discussion at that wonderful conference when there was a
statement put forward about the Pacific, Pacific nations said: “We do not want your idea
of development.” Country after country got up and said about this important
relationship around overseas development and around assistance and around trade: “We
reject your model. We want to protect our resources.” Vanuatu was the first speaker. I
can quote you the speech. And they were the first people to say it, but country after
country got up and said:  “We know that the natural resources of our world need to be
protected. We know that they are vulnerable. We know that our relationship with
Australasia and Aotearoa is important. But we want overseas development and
assistance that actually allows us to p rotect our resources.” They do not want the Trans -
Pacific Partnership agreement any more than many of us in this country do.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I just want to touch on the spe ech from
Nicky Wagner from before. What she failed to talk about in her speech was the
JBMS—the Joint Border Management System —that her Customs Service has been
overseeing. It has run off-budget—$30 million off-budget. It has not delivered what she
said it was going to deliver, and now we have the old system and the new system —the
CusMod system and the Joint Border Management System —running side by side,
duplicating each other’s work. What a shemozzle. And if that was not the only thing
wrong with the Customs Service, here is another thing: there is the highest number of
churn through that department than any other Government department, and there is the
lowest morale in the Customs Service. There are serious things wrong with the Customs
Service. It is the staff who are not happy and the information systems that have failed,
and that is what this Minister of Customs is not getting on to.
5384 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
But, anyway, I want to move on to foreign affairs. We came on to the United Nations
Security Council this year. It is good that New Zealand is represented there. We were all
very proud of that, and we are currently, right now, this month, in the presidency—there
is a rotating presidency, and New Zealand holds the presidency in the United Nations
Security Council. Murray McCully said that there were three things he wanted to do: he
wanted to solve the Middle East peace process, he wanted to solve the issue of the veto
in the United Nations Security Council, and he wanted to do some work on bringing up
the issues and the intere sts of small, developing States. Well, we have not heard
anything about small, developing States; we have heard a bit about solving the Middle
East peace process, and at the moment we have got 3 days left in July and we still have
not quite got on top of i t; and we still have not knocked off the veto in the United
Nations Security Council. This may play well to a New Zealand audience, but to an
international audience it sounds woefully out of touch and incredibly naive. We can,
obviously, do some work to pr ogress these issues, but coming out and saying somehow
New Zealand is going to turn those things round is —well, look, I wish him all the best,
but in anybody’s reckoning it is wishful thinking.
Meanwhile, the Government has done this —and I want to just run through this little
story. There are 900 sheep in the South Island, 300 owned by Mr Al Ali Khalaf. The
Government and Murray McCully, really without very much consultation with any of
his colleagues, decided to buy 300 sheep for Mr Al Ali Khalaf, fly the m courtesy of
Singapore Airlines to Saudi Arabia to Mr Al Ali Khalaf’s farm, and give them to Mr Al
Ali Khalaf. Can you believe that? This is a true story. This is a true story. You could
write about this and nobody would believe you. And then those 900 sheep that sit there
in Saudi Arabia are all pregnant ewes, and 700 of their lambs die. This is supposed to be
a model farm that New Zealand is going to be advertising its wares from. Incredible —
what an incredible fiasco and debacle.
The reason we did that, according to the Government, is because the Labour
Government said that we were banning the export of live sheep, and it had upset Mr Al
Ali Khalaf. Well, actually, this Government extended the ban on live sheep exports in
2010, but somehow that was the problem. Mr Al Ali Khalaf was supposed to be suing
New Zealand because we had taken away some of his rights. The only thing is that the
Government will not release the papers that show what Mr Al Ali Khalaf was likely to
do. Mr McCully says: “Oh, we actuall y had a legal opinion on this.” Well, he will not
release the legal opinion, and they certainly will not release any information about
whether they sought a second legal opinion, perhaps from the Crown Law Office —
absolute debacle.
But then there is anothe r reason. There is another reason, and that reason is that
somehow this is going to block a free -trade agreement that New Zealand is going to
have with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf States. I want you to reflect on this: if a
company had said that they were going to be paying a Saudi businessman this sort of
money, what would we call it? We would call it a bribe. That is what we would call it
and that is exactly what it is, and yet Mr McCully has entered the New Zealand
Government into a bribe.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to
take a call in this part of the debate on Vote Foreign Affairs and Trade. Particularly, I
would like to commend, I suppose, all of the members of the Foreign Affairs, Defence
and Trade Committee for the useful report that they have put together. Of course, we
have heard from other speakers about the great accomplishments in the area of the
foreign affairs  of New Zealand and, therefore, the Government and the Minister of
Foreign Affairs, Murray McCully, over the last year. Of course, that is about our
accession—our moving up and being elected—to the UN Security Council.
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5385
Over the 3 or 4 or 5 years that Mr Mc Cully and Sir Jim McLay and others were
campaigning on behalf of New Zealand for this seat on the Security Council, there were
members of this House who said that it would never happen. They said that New
Zealand would not get the recognition that Minister  McCully was seeking, and some
said that it was a waste of effort, a waste of time, and —dare I say it —a waste of
taxpayers’ money. I think that it is a significant accomplishment on the part of New
Zealand to be elected to the Security Council, not only on the first vote but also with so
many votes to spare. The reason why the support that New Zealand received was so
significant is that we are seen to be a fair -minded country that will stand up for the
rights of people all round the world. We set out an age nda and said that we would go
and talk about those issues, and we received that significant support.
I know that every member of this House, bar a few, supports Mr McCully in his
work and is certainly very proud that New Zealand has been recognised and has
received the votes of so many countries of the world. I know that inside this Chamber is
a political place, but listening to some of the speeches during this part of the debate, it
would lead one to believe that not all of the support that should be backi ng New
Zealand is as obvious and apparent as it might or should be from members of the
Opposition. I put that down to the politics of the situation. I know that David Shearer is
a very big supporter of New Zealand’s place on the United Nations, and he is a  man for
whom I have a lot of respect —a lot of respect for Mr Shearer. Indeed, he spoke about
customs and his concern about the very high churn of officials in the Customs Service. I
was of a mind not to believe him but then I realised, actually, that he has a lot of
experience in this area. Nowhere else across the Government or within this Parliament
has there been more churn than with Mr Shearer and all of those other Labour Party
leaders who have rotated through that seat over the past 6 years.
Mr Sheare r said that he was supportive of Mr McCully, but then he offered some
words of wisdom about what he should actually be doing over there. This is the same
Mr Shearer who jumped on a plane to go and support Mr McCully just after, I think, the
election last year, and who was the very first person to put out a press release following
the vote, congratulating Mr McCully —not congratulating New Zealand or the
Government, but saying that he had been able to do some important work in the day that
he had been there t hat had helped to deliver this victory for New Zealand. That was Mr
Shearer. Putting that aside, actually, I know that his heart is in the right place and that
he is one of the few members on that side of the Chamber who are actually willing to
put what is  important for New Zealand first, even when it comes to—and this is my
second intervention, when I want to talk more about trade —being supportive of high-
quality trade agreements. I know that when many of his colleagues vote against the
Trans-Pacific Partnership, he will be conflicted. I would not mind betting that we will
see him on this side of the House.
We have taken on the UN Security Council presidency at the moment, and Mr
McCully, with our representatives there, is representing New Zealand extremely well.
There are two other parts that I want to speak about in this report. The first is our
relationship with the ASEAN countries. In 2015 there will be the 40 th anniversary of
New Zealand’s diplomatic relations with ASEAN, and that is quite some achievement.
In fact, we have very important relationships with all of those countries. Indeed, New
Zealand will host 31 celebratory events across 10 Asian capitals, with representatives
from these countries, to celebrate that relationship and the important trading
relationships that we have with them. But it goes so much further than that —many of
those ASEAN countries supported us towards the UN.
A final bit here is about Niue and our relationship with it —the smallest country in
the world and a very special relationship for New Zealand. Mr McCully has
5386 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015
championed our relationship and has ensured that we give the right type of support to
Niue, and, in particular, since 2010 a lot of effort between the Governments has gone
into the promotion of tourism.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to
make a brief call in defence of Defence Force personnel during the debate on the
external sector in the Committee stage of the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill. I
have to say I subbed briefly on to the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee to
take the opportunity to hear the Minister of Defence, who made a presentation along
with the Chief of Defence Force, Tim Keating, so that I could get a bit of clarification
around why I could not find in the appropriations a clear indica tion or any detail of a
pay increase for Defence Force personnel. I think it is only appropriate at this time to
remind the Committee that it was not so long ago when we had a certain gentleman
standing on that side of the Chamber yelling at the House —in fact, I actually believe it
was outside the Standing Orders myself, but the Speaker never responded—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Do not relitigate that, please. Carry
on.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: He did not respond, Mr Chair. The question was put to this side of the
House that we should gain some intestinal fortitude; in fact, that we should “get some
guts”. The question put across the House was about how the Opposition needed to get
some guts and support the deployment of these troops. Often in my time in the Defence
Force—15 years in the New Zealand Army and 5 years operating internationally —I
heard many, many speakers from this House talking about how they valued Defence
Force people. In fact, if I summed up the number of minutes of speeches at Anzac Day
services by Government MPs and Ministers from both sides of the House —Labour or
National; both the same to me —talking about how they valued Defence Force
contributions, I mean, if I had a dollar  for every second I would not be here today; I
would be retired.
What we now know from the appropriations is that despite the calls to get some guts
and despite the accolades poured upon the Defence Force, it did not seem to be enough
to move this Governm ent to give personnel a pay rise. There is nothing in this Budget
for a pay rise for Defence Force personnel. In fact, when I look a little bit deeper, what
do we in New Zealand First find? We find that this Government, actually, has the
legislative tools and the mechanisms to do one thing for our Defence Force personnel —
those deployed to Iraq who have got the guts to go—and that is to give them a tax -free
wage. Australia has done it, the United States has done it, but not the New Zealand
Government. When I  asked the Minister of Defence that very question in the select
committee, his answer was no, they didn’t consider that. New Zealand First’s question
is why not. If these Defence Force personnel are so vital to the foreign policy of this
nation and so vita l to foreign policy in the view of this Government, then why can this
Government not see fit to pay them a tax-free wage, as the legislation, Minister Bennett,
allows your Cabinet to do. She is mouthing at me across the Chamber —take a call,
answer my quest ion. As opposed to just chipping at me and mouthing across the
Chamber, Minister Bennett, tell the people of New Zealand and the people at Linton
Military Camp and Burnham Military Camp why this Government chose not to.
If I look at the Cabinet committee that is meant to advocate on behalf of these
Defence Force people—the people whom the Government values so much, the people
that it wants to pour so many accolades on but is too cheapskate to actually pay them
what they are worth—who do I find on this comm ittee? Oh, the ministerial committee
that makes this determination includes the Prime Minister John Key —well, he clearly
did not think that they deserved a pay rise. He clearly did not think that they deserved a
tax-free wage for being in Iraq. There is th e Minister of Defence—well, who is going to
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5387
expect a hell of a lot of support from that gentleman —and there is the Minister of
Finance. I am surprised about Bill English. I had almost picked that Bill English was on
his own. Section CW23(3) of the Income T ax Act states that the ministerial committee,
which also includes the Minister of Foreign Affairs, “may, for the purposes of
subsection (2)(b), decide that an amount of income derived by a member for being in an
operational area is exempt income.” But this  Government, no matter what it says out
there on the hustings, no matter what it says in the media, and no matter what it says in
the House, cannot find it within itself to pay our troops in Iraq today a tax-free salary.
What would that do? Well, let me tell you, as someone who has deployed, unlike the
person who is yelling out across the House —he would not know what deployment
meant—

items.speaker: Alastair Scott
items.text: Can you spell it?

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: What I can tell you is about when the husbands, the wives, those
service personnel are offshore—listen up, Alastair Scott. When they are offshore it is
left down to the spouse remaining to look after the kids, to pay the power bill, to pay the
rent—now that they are subject to market rents, because the hous es have been taken
away from them by this Government —pay all off those bills and deal with the coughs,
the colds, the trauma that normally comes up in raising a family. It is hard to do as a
couple. It is even harder to do when one is on one’s own. It is e ven harder to do if one’s
spouse is deployed in Iraq and cannot get back. When all those things come to a head it
is left down to the spouse back here at home, and it is left down to this Government to
have some heart and recognise that.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
speak in this debate. I just want to contrast that last speaker, Ron Mark. The members of
the public out there will know him as probably one of the most angry members of this
House, and a most detestable member of this House as well. But that member was
actually part of a Government that sent troops overseas and did not give them tax -free
salaries. Why did that Government not give t hem a tax -free salary? Why did the
Government that that member was part of not give them a tax -free salary? When that
member was in Government, troops were sent overseas without tax-free status.
And then today, in this Chamber, he comes here and says: “Look at me. I am the
person standing up for those troops. I am the person who is the only one who cares. I
am the only one who is doing this.” And when he had a chance he delivered nothing for
those troops. All he did was pay for his big fat salary so that he  could walk behind his
leader and leave this Chamber whenever his leader instructs him to do something.
Never has that member delivered anything for this country, in this Parliament. Never
has that member actually delivered anything that an individual memb er of Parliament
would do. All that member has done in his whole lifetime is sit behind somebody else
and be on their gravy train. That is all that member knows.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I need to assist, as a point of
correction. I was in a National -  New Zealand First coalition Government that delivered
lots of good things for the people of New Zealand.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: That is not a point of order; it is a
matter of debate. The member will be seated.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Thank you. When we come to the foreign affairs and defence
areas of this country—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Which you’d know very little about.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Mr Cosgrove is over there. Mr Cosgrove is another member
who knows all about sitting on the fat of the country, is he not? We would like to see
him win a seat back in that area again, but that is not going to happen, is it, Mr
Cosgrove? Coming in here spouting, as well—
5388 Estimates Debate 28 Jul 2015

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Go back to San Francisco.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I would be quiet, Mr Mark, because the public has seen your
true colours tonight. The public has seen somebody that is not black and white. He is
not New Zealand First. He is not even Green. Ha, ha! He is another colour, and the
reason that he is that colour is that he does not stand up for the people of New Zealand
when he has a chance, and that is the reality of it. And the Labour Party—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Back to the bill—back to the bill.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: OK, but it is not really a bill. It is the estimates, but I will get
back to it.
When we talk in this debate about foreign a ffairs, it is important to look at New
Zealand as an open, free country, a country that is confident to take its place on the
world stage, a country that New Zealanders can be proud of, and proud of what it stands
for, and a country that is open to people coming here and making their lives in this
country. New Zealand is a country that sees a future in the Asia -Pacific region. It is a
country that does not want to discriminate against people on the basis of their surnames.
It is a country that does not want to discriminate—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The member is debating the
estimates; it would be good if he got back to them.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: OK, Mr Chair. I know Mr Mark wants to clap, but t hat is what
he does when he is that member of the party, and I would love for Tracey Martin to be
here at this stage, as well. The estimates are an important part of what we look at when
we look at what this country is achieving on the world stage, especia lly in the defence
area and in the foreign affairs area. When we look at the speeches made in the past, they
have talked about things like New Zealand’s role on the Security Council, they have
talked about free -trade agreements with Korea, and they have ta lked about free -trade
agreements that are soon to come, which the Green Party will be voting against, and
which the Labour Party, for the first time in its history, will be voting against. It will be
voting against free trade and against something that wil l deliver for New Zealanders,
and that is a shame on the Labour Party.
You just have to go across the Ditch to see that it did not work out when people took
that attitude towards the ability of a country to trade and become more successful. New
Zealanders need those trade arrangements. They need those trade agreements, and it is a
shame on the Labour Party that its leadership will be ideologically driven to oppose free
trade—just as they are opposed to immigration, just as they are opposed to people
making New Zealand their home, and just as they are opposed to this country taking its
rightful place in foreign affairs and taking its rightful place in the Asia -Pacific region.
We can be a leader in that region. We can be a country that is seen as free, indepen dent,
and confident, and one that delivers for its people. We do not have to be seen as a
country that is insular, against trade, against immigration, and against people making a
future for themselves in this country, as the Opposition parties have shown t hemselves
to be tonight in their speeches and in their failure to act when given the chance to many
years ago.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: I almost did not want to
interrupt the member David Bennett. That was one of the most insightful and thought -
provoking speeches I have heard in this Chamber for some time. I congratulate him on
that. As he is the chair of our most significant committee in this Parliament w e are in
very good hands.
I want to talk now about trade and the importance of trade. Not everybody in this
Parliament understands the importance of trade to New Zealand. We do not become
richer from selling to ourselves. Of all the things we produce so well, be it from dairy,
wood, and wood processing —all of these areas —we produce more than we can
28 Jul 2015 Estimates Debate 5389
consume in New Zealand. We are a trading nation. To be able to make sure that our
producers can trade successfully, to make sure that New Zealanders can retain their
jobs, we need high- quality, broad trade agreements that at the very least give us the
same advantage that some of our competitors have into some of the most competitive
markets in the world. But in many cases a free-trade agreement gives us an advantage, a
preference.
Over th e last year New Zealand has achieved a significant amount in trade
negotiations, but also when it comes to trade. Last year New Zealand exported $55
billion worth of goods and services, a significant increase on the previous year. That is
the first thing. The second thing is that when one looks at the top 10 countries of
